chapters.title: Fluid Mechanics
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the fundamental concepts of fluid mechanics, beginning with the classification of matter and the properties that distinguish fluids from solids. It covers pressure in fluids, fluid statics, and the behavior of incompressible, nonviscous liquids under various conditions.

events.text: Solid — strong intermolecular forces → fixed shape AND fixed volume
Liquid — weaker forces → shape changes freely, volume stays fixed
Fluids = liquids + gases (both flow; liquids are nearly incompressible)
Ideal fluid: force between layers is always perpendicular — no sideways friction
Incompressible + non-viscous: the two assumptions we carry forward
Pressure = Force ÷ Area (as area → 0)
Pressure has NO direction — same in all orientations
F1 (up) = P·ΔS
F2 (down) = (P+dP)·ΔS
dP/dz = −ρg
Deeper → more weight above → higher pressure
Q: Derive how pressure varies with height in a static fluid, and find the pressure difference between two levels separated by height h.
Forces on enclosed fluid:
F1 (upward, from fluid below)  = P × ΔS
F2 (downward, from fluid above) = (P + dP) × ΔS
W  (downward weight)           = ρ × ΔS × dz × g
Vertical equilibrium: F1 = F2 + W
⟹  P × ΔS = (P + dP) × ΔS + ρg dz ΔS
⟹  dP = −ρ g dz
Integrate from z = 0 (pressure P1) to z = h (pressure P2):
∫dP = −∫ρg dz  ⟹  P2 − P1 = −ρgh   (uniform density)
P1 − P2 = ρ g h  (pressure difference between two levels of height h in a uniform-density fluid)
Q: Two points A and B lie at the same horizontal level inside a fluid in equilibrium. Show that the pressure at A equals the pressure at B.
Force on left end  = P₁ × S  (directed right)
Force on right end = P₂ × S  (directed left)
Equilibrium condition:  P₁S = P₂S
P₁ = P₂  →  Pressure is the same at any two points on the same horizontal level.
SI unit: pascal (Pa) = N per m²
Pressure diff between 2 pts = density × g × depth difference
Pascal's Law: pressure change at one point → same change at EVERY point

Q: A flask fitted with a piston of cross-sectional area A is filled with liquid. An external force F is applied on the piston. By how much does the pressure increase at a point B located a vertical distance z below the piston?
Pressure increase at piston = F / A
Pressure at B = Pressure at piston + (rho × g × z)
Pressure increase at B = F / A   (same as at the piston, because z is unchanged)

Q: A hydraulic lift has two vertical cylinders A and B with cross-sectional areas A1 and A2. A force F1 is applied to the narrow piston A. What force F2 is produced on the wider piston B, and is any energy gained?
Pressure increase = F1 / A1   (transmitted equally throughout the liquid)
Work done by F1 = Work done by F2   (no energy gain)
Force multiplication: F_out = f × (A/a)
Air pushes equally in all directions
More air above = higher pressure below
Column falls to ~76 cm, then stops
Atmospheric pressure = weight of 76 cm mercury column
Vacuum top → P_top = 0
Q: Water fills a flask to height h = 0.20 m, circular bottom radius r = 0.10 m. Atmospheric pressure P₀ = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, g = 10 m/s², ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Find force on the bottom.
P = P₀ + h·ρ·g
F = 3230 newtons
Q: A barometer shows a mercury column height of seventy-six centimeters. What is the atmospheric pressure in pascals?
P₀ = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa = 1 atm
Barometer: atmosphere pushes open surface → holds column up

events.title: Buoyancy — the upward push of a fluid

events.text: Fluid presses on every face of a submerged object
Deeper → higher pressure → stronger upward push
How big is the buoyant force?
Replace body with same-shaped fluid → equilibrium
Buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid
Same boundary → same contact forces → same B
Archimedes' principle follows from Newton's laws
B depends on: fluid density × submerged volume × g
Q: A 700 gram solid cube with edge length 10 centimeters floats in water. How much of the cube's volume is outside the water? Density of water equals 1000 kilograms per cubic meter.
Buoyant force = weight of displaced water = V × ρ × g
V × ρ × g = 0.7 kg × g
Total volume = 10³ = 1000 cm³
Volume outside water = 1000 − 700 = 300 cm³
Volume outside water = 300 cubic centimeters
B = weight of displaced fluid — the one rule for floating and sinking
Forces on fluid cylinder: P1·S up, P2·S down, mg down
P1·S − P2·S − mg = m·a0
P1 − P2 = ρ(g + a₀)z — effective gravity replaces g

events.title: Buoyant Force in an Accelerating Fluid

events.text: Q: A beaker of liquid is in an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Points A and B are in the liquid, with B at vertical height z above A. The liquid has density rho. Find the pressure difference P1 minus P2 between A and B.
Forces on the cylinder (vertical direction):
(a) P1 times S — upward, from liquid below
(b) P2 times S — downward, from liquid above
(c) weight = S times z times rho times g — downward
Newton's second law (upward positive):
P1·S − P2·S − S·z·rho·g = S·z·rho·a0
(P1 − P2)·S = S·z·rho·g + S·z·rho·a0
P1 − P2 = rho·(g + a0)·z
P1 − P2 = rho × (g + a0) × z
Q: A body is fully submerged in a liquid of density rho, inside an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Find the buoyant force B on the body.
Substituted liquid: mass m = mass of displaced liquid, accelerating upward at a0
Forces on substituted liquid: (a) Buoyant force B — upward, (b) Weight mg — downward
Newton's second law → B − mg = m times a0
Rearranging → B = m times g + m times a0 = m times (g + a0)
B = m(g + a0), where m is the mass of the displaced liquid

Q: A beaker of liquid accelerates horizontally with acceleration a0. Points A and B are at the same horizontal level, separated by distance l along the direction of acceleration. The liquid has density rho. Find the tilt angle theta of the free surface.
(P1 − P2)ΔS = (ΔS) · l · ρ · a0
P1 − P2 = l · ρ · a0
P1 = P0 + h1·ρ·g,   P2 = P0 + h2·ρ·g
tan θ = (h1 − h2) / l = a0 / g
tan θ = a0 / g  (theta = tilt angle of the free surface)
Buoyant force = ρV(g + a₀) in accelerating fluid
Free fall: a₀ = −g → buoyancy = 0
Each droplet: F = ma, every moment
Billions of droplets → billions of interactions
Complexity comes from interactions, not from the rules
Fluid flow: simple laws, staggering complexity
Steady flow → every particle through A follows the same streamline
Streamlines never cross each other
Steady flow = velocity at each point constant in time
Turbulent flow → velocity at same point changes erratically
Slow → steady (streamline). Fast → turbulent
Assumption 1 — Incompressible: density same everywhere, always
Assumption 2 — Nonviscous: no internal friction
Assumption 3 — Irrotational: no particle spins about its own axis
Irrotational ≠ straight-line flow. It means no individual particle self-spins.
Ideal fluid = incompressible + nonviscous + irrotational → no energy loss, maths stays clean.
Fluid in one tube never mixes with fluid in another
Mass in = Mass out (conservation of mass)
A₁v₁Δt = A₂v₂Δt
A₁v₁ = A₂v₂  (Equation of Continuity)
Q: Piston area A1 = 1.0 cm², outlet area A2 = 20 mm², piston speed v1 = 2 cm/s. Find v2.
A₁v₁ = A₂v₂
(1.0 cm²)(2 cm/s) = (20 mm²) × v₂
v₂ = (1.0 cm² / 20 mm²) × 2 cm/s
v₂ = (100 mm² / 20 mm²) × 2 cm/s
v₂ = 10 cm/s
Av = constant everywhere in tube
Net work = (P1 − P2) × Δm/ρ
W_pressure = ΔKE + ΔPE
ΔKE = ½Δm(v₂² − v₁²), ΔPE = Δmg(h₂ − h₁)

events.latex: P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2

events.text: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant

Q: A liquid of density one thousand two hundred kilograms per cubic meter flows steadily through a tube. The cross-sectional area at point A is one point zero square centimeters, and at point B it is twenty square millimeters. Points A and B are at the same horizontal height. The speed at A is ten centimeters per second. Find the difference in pressures at A and B.
Continuity: A1·v1 = A2·v2
v2 = (100 mm² × 10 cm/s) ÷ 20 mm² = 50 cm/s
P1 + ρgh1 + ½ρv1² = P2 + ρgh2 + ½ρv2²
Since h1 = h2 → P1 − P2 = ½ρ(v2² − v1²)
v2² = 2500 cm²/s²,  v1² = 100 cm²/s²
= 600 kg/m³ × 2400 cm²/s²
P1 − P2 = 144 pascals
Faster flow → lower pressure
Point 1: top surface (open to air)
v1 ≈ 0 since tank area
ρgh = ½ρv₂² → v₂ = √(2gh)
Torricelli's Theorem: v = √(2gh) — same as free fall!
v=0 everywhere → P1 + ρgh1 = P2 + ρgh2

Q: A water tank sits on top of a building. With what speed does water come out of a tap six point zero meters below the water level in the tank? Assume steady flow, and that the pressure above the water level equals atmospheric pressure.
v ≈ 11 m/s (approximately eleven meters per second)

Q: Water flows through a horizontal tube. The pressure difference between points A and B is six hundred newtons per meter squared. The cross-sectional area at A is thirty centimeters squared and at B is fifteen centimeters squared. Find the rate of flow of water. (Density of water = one thousand kilograms per meter cubed.)
Continuity: v_B / v_A = 30 cm² / 15 cm² = 2  →  v_B = 2 v_A
Bernoulli (horizontal): P_A + ½ρv_A² = P_B + ½ρv_B²
P_A − P_B = ½ρ(v_B² − v_A²)
= ½ρ(2v_A)² − ½ρv_A² = (3/2)ρv_A²
Rate of flow = 30 cm² × 0.63 m/s ≈ 1890 cm³/s

Q: A tank has a cross-sectional area of zero point five meters squared and a small opening near the bottom with area one centimeter squared. A load of twenty kilograms sits on the water surface. The water level is fifty centimeters above the opening. Find the exit velocity of the water. Take g as ten meters per second squared.
P_A = P₀ + 400 N/m²
P_A + ρgh + ½ρv_A² = P_B + ½ρv_B²
5400 N/m² = 500 kg/m³ × v_B²
v_B ≈ 3.3 meters per second
Bernoulli → hydrostatics when v = 0 everywhere

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_1>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> You can crush an empty plastic bottle with your hand — but try squeezing a sealed syringe full of water and it barely moves. Why does water resist being squished, yet pours so freely? The answer lives inside the molecule. <<FOCUS:solid-molecules>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_1:states_of_matter>> <<SECTION:Three States of Matter|id=sec-1>>Let's look at the three states of matter side by side. Here are the molecules in a solid — packed tightly in a neat grid, each one gripping its neighbours with strong forces. <<WRITE_TEXT:Solid — strong intermolecular forces → fixed shape AND fixed volume|id=text-1>>Those strong forces mean a brick keeps its shape and its size no matter which container you drop it into. Shape: locked. Volume: locked. <<POINT:solid-label>> <<FOCUS:liquid-molecules>> Now look at a liquid. The molecules are still touching, still attracted to each other — but the grip is weaker. Watch what that means. <<WRITE_TEXT:Liquid — weaker forces → shape changes freely, volume stays fixed|id=text-2>>Because the grip is looser, molecules can slide past each other — pour water into any bottle and it takes that shape instantly. But here is the key: the molecules are still close enough that squeezing them tighter takes enormous effort. The volume barely budges. <<TRACE:liquid-molecules>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:gas-molecules>> And in a gas — molecules are flying around nearly free of each other. Shape: gone. Volume: gone. Push a gas and it compresses happily. <<FOCUS:force-strength-bar>> <<WRITE_KEY:Fluids = liquids + gases (both flow; liquids are nearly incompressible)|id=key-1>>So here is the definition that ties it together: anything that flows is a fluid. Liquids flow. Gases flow. Both are fluids. But only liquids are nearly incompressible — their density stays essentially constant no matter how hard you push on them. <<POINT:force-strength-bar>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:liquid-molecules>> <<SECTION:How Fluids Push|id=sec-2>>Now here is something worth pausing on. When two layers of a liquid are in contact, how do they push on each other? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Ideal fluid: force between layers is always perpendicular — no sideways friction|id=text-3>>The force is always perpendicular — at right angles — to the surface between them. Never sideways. This means there is no friction between layers of an ideal fluid. The layers glide past each other without any drag. <<TRACE:liquid-molecules>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Incompressible + non-viscous: the two assumptions we carry forward|id=key-2>>These two ideas — incompressible volume and no friction between layers — are the two assumptions we carry into every problem in this chapter. They are what makes the maths clean and the physics beautiful. <<POINT:liquid-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So next time you pour water into a glass, remember: it flows freely because the molecular grip is loose enough to let layers slide — but it will not compress because those same molecules are already as close as they want to be. That tension between 'flows easily' and 'resists squeezing' is exactly what makes liquids so fascinating — and so useful in engineering.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_2>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Why does your ear pop when you dive deep into a pool — but not when you tilt your head sideways at the same depth? That single observation is going to unlock everything about pressure in a fluid. <<FOCUS:point-a>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_2:pressure_point>> <<SECTION:Pressure at a Point|id=sec-1>>Let's pick any point inside a body of fluid — call it point A. Now imagine a tiny flat patch of area sitting around that point. The fluid on one side of the patch shoves the fluid on the other side, and the other side shoves back. The force per unit area — as we shrink that patch down to nothing — is what we call the pressure at point A. <<WRITE_TEXT:Pressure = Force ÷ Area (as area → 0)|id=text-1>>So pressure is defined as P equals the limit of F divided by delta S, as delta S shrinks to zero. It's the force squeezing through an infinitely small window of area. <<POINT:area-horizontal>> Pressure at a point is the force pushing through a tiny area patch, divided by that area, as the patch shrinks to essentially nothing. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P = \lim_{\Delta S \to 0} \frac{F}{\Delta S}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:area-tilted>> Now here's the really surprising part. What if we tilt that tiny patch? Rotate it forty-five degrees, or ninety degrees, or any angle at all — the pressure value doesn't change. For a smooth fluid with no internal friction, the pressure at a point is completely independent of which direction you face your little area patch. <<TRACE:area-tilted>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Pressure has NO direction — same in all orientations|id=key-1>>That's what it means to say pressure is a scalar. Not a vector. No arrow. No direction. Just a number — the same number no matter which way you slice through the fluid at that point. That's exactly why your ears feel equally squeezed from every direction when you're deep underwater. <<POINT:equal-pressure-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:fluid-column>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_2:pressure_depth>> <<SECTION:Pressure vs Depth|id=sec-2>>Now for the next question: does pressure change as you move up or down in a fluid? <<PAUSE:long>> Picture a short slab of fluid trapped between two horizontal layers — layer A at the bottom and layer B at the top, separated by a tiny height dz. Three forces act on this slab vertically. The fluid below pushes it up with force F one. The fluid above pushes it down with force F two. And gravity pulls the slab's own weight straight down. <<TRACE:fluid-column>> <<POINT:fluid-column>> <<FOCUS:f1-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:F1 (up) = P·ΔS|id=step-1>>F one pushing up equals the pressure P at level A times the area delta S. And F two pushing down equals the pressure at level B — call it P plus dP — times the same area. <<FOCUS:f2-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:F2 (down) = (P+dP)·ΔS|id=step-2>>The slab isn't accelerating — it's just sitting there in equilibrium. So the net upward force must be zero. That means F one minus F two minus W equals zero. <<FOCUS:weight-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:dP/dz = −ρg|id=step-3>>The weight W of the slab is density rho times g times the volume, which is delta S times dz. When you substitute everything in and simplify, you get: dP equals negative rho times g times dz. The negative sign tells you pressure drops as you go UP — or equivalently, pressure rises as you go DOWN. <<POINT:weight-arrow>> The pressure change over a tiny vertical distance equals negative the fluid density times gravitational acceleration — so pressure falls as you rise, and grows as you descend. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dP}{dz} = -\rho g|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Deeper → more weight above → higher pressure|id=key-2>>Think about it physically: every extra meter of water above you adds more weight pressing down. That's all the equation is saying. Dive twice as deep, and there's twice as much water sitting on top of you, so the pressure is roughly twice as large. <<TRACE:depth-gradient-label>> <<POINT:depth-gradient-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter that builds the core result for pressure variation with depth. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Derive how pressure varies with height in a static fluid, and find the pressure difference between two levels separated by height h.|id=ex-q-1>> We consider two horizontal surfaces — call them delta S one and delta S two — separated by a small vertical height d z. Point A sits on the lower surface, and point B sits on the upper surface. The pressure at lower surface A is P, and the pressure at upper surface B is P plus d P. Now let's identify the three vertical forces acting on the fluid enclosed between those two surfaces. <<WRITE_STEP:Forces on enclosed fluid:|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:F1 (upward, from fluid below)  = P × ΔS|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:F2 (downward, from fluid above) = (P + dP) × ΔS|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:W  (downward weight)           = ρ × ΔS × dz × g|id=ex-step-1-4>> The upward force F one equals P times delta S, the downward force F two equals open bracket P plus d P close bracket times delta S, and the weight W of the enclosed fluid equals rho times delta S times d z times g, since the volume of that little slab is delta S times d z. For the fluid to be in vertical equilibrium, the upward force must balance the two downward forces. So we write F one equals F two plus W. <<WRITE_STEP:Vertical equilibrium: F1 = F2 + W|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<WRITE_STEP:⟹  P × ΔS = (P + dP) × ΔS + ρg dz ΔS|id=ex-step-1-6>> Expanding the right-hand side, P times delta S equals P times delta S plus d P times delta S plus rho times g times d z times delta S. The P times delta S terms cancel on both sides, and dividing through by delta S we get d P equals negative rho times g times d z. <<WRITE_STEP:⟹  dP = −ρ g dz|id=ex-step-1-7>> This tells us that as we move upward through a height d z, the pressure decreases by rho times g times d z — pressure decreases as height increases. Now we integrate this result between two levels. Take z equals zero at the bottom with pressure P one, and z equals h at the top with pressure P two. <<WRITE_STEP:Integrate from z = 0 (pressure P1) to z = h (pressure P2):|id=ex-step-1-8>> <<WRITE_STEP:∫dP = −∫ρg dz  ⟹  P2 − P1 = −ρgh   (uniform density)|id=ex-step-1-9>> For a fluid of uniform density rho, the integral on the right is just rho times g times h, giving P two minus P one equals negative rho times g times h, or equivalently P one minus P two equals rho times g times h. And there is our key result. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:P1 − P2 = ρ g h  (pressure difference between two levels of height h in a uniform-density fluid)|id=ex-ans-1>> The pressure difference between any two horizontal levels in a uniform-density fluid equals rho times g times h, where h is the vertical height separating them. The deeper level always has the higher pressure, which is exactly what we expect: every extra layer of fluid above you adds weight, and that weight drives the pressure up. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Two points A and B lie at the same horizontal level inside a fluid in equilibrium. Show that the pressure at A equals the pressure at B.|id=ex-q-1>> Consider two points A and B at the same horizontal level inside a fluid. We imagine a small vertical area S containing point A, and an equal small vertical area S containing point B — so both cross-sectional areas are the same value, which we call S. Now picture the horizontal cylinder of fluid that connects the two points — it's bounded on the left by area S at point A and on the right by area S at point B. The fluid to the left pushes on this cylinder with a force equal to P one times S, directed towards the right. The fluid to the right pushes back with a force equal to P two times S, directed towards the left. <<WRITE_STEP:Force on left end  = P₁ × S  (directed right)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Force on right end = P₂ × S  (directed left)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Because the fluid is in equilibrium, these two forces must balance each other exactly. So the equilibrium condition gives us P one times S equals P two times S. <<WRITE_STEP:Equilibrium condition:  P₁S = P₂S|id=ex-step-1-3>> We can divide both sides by S, and S cancels out completely, leaving us with P one equals P two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:P₁ = P₂  →  Pressure is the same at any two points on the same horizontal level.|id=ex-ans-1>> And that is the conclusion: any two points at the same horizontal level inside a fluid in equilibrium have exactly the same pressure. <<PAUSE:short>> So here's the payoff to our opening mystery: your ears pop going deeper because there's more fluid above you — more weight, more pressure — and that pressure squeezes from every direction at once, because pressure at a point is a scalar with no preferred direction. <<POINT:dz-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:SI unit: pascal (Pa) = N per m²|id=text-2>>One last thing to lock in: pressure is measured in pascals. One pascal equals one newton per square meter. It's named after Blaise Pascal — who, not coincidentally, is exactly the person we'll talk about in the next topic.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_3>>
<<FOCUS:small-piston>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_3:hydraulic_lift>> A single finger — pushing on a small piston — can lift a one-tonne car. The liquid in between doesn't cheat, it doesn't store energy, it doesn't do magic. So how on earth does that work? <<FOCUS:depth-arrow>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_3:flask_piston>> <<SECTION:Pressure in a still liquid|id=sec-1>>Before we answer that, remember what you already know: in a liquid sitting perfectly still, the pressure at any point depends only on how deep that point is. Go deeper, pressure goes up — by a fixed, predictable amount. <<WRITE_TEXT:Pressure diff between 2 pts = density × g × depth difference|id=text-1>>The pressure difference between two points is fixed — it depends on their vertical separation, the density of the liquid, and the gravitational pull. Nothing else. That gap is locked in. <<POINT:depth-arrow>> <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> <<SECTION:What happens when you push?|id=sec-2>>Now here's the key question: what if you push down on this liquid with a piston — forcing extra pressure in from outside? What happens to that pressure difference between the two points? <<POINT:force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:point-B-delta-label>> The liquid is essentially incompressible — the depth z between the piston and point B barely changes when you push. So the pressure difference between them must stay exactly the same. But the pressure at the piston just went up by F divided by A. Therefore the pressure at B must also go up by exactly F divided by A. <<TRACE:point-B-delta-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:pressure-delta-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Pascal's Law: pressure change at one point → same change at EVERY point|id=key-1>>That's Pascal's Law. Any change in pressure you apply at one point travels through the entire liquid — to every single point — without losing any of its strength. <<POINT:pressure-delta-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> The extra pressure injected into the liquid equals the pushing force divided by the area of the piston — and that extra pressure is felt at every single point in the liquid. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Delta p = \frac{F}{A}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:pressure-delta-label>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Delta p_{\text{applied}} = \frac{F}{A}|id=eq-1>>We can write this cleanly: the extra pressure added equals the applied force divided by the piston's cross-sectional area. That pressure boost — every point in the liquid feels it instantly and equally. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:liquid-body>> <<SECTION:The hydraulic lift|id=sec-3>>Now let's return to that finger lifting a car. This is a hydraulic machine. On the left, a small piston with area a. On the right, a large piston with area A — much bigger. Both connected by the same liquid. <<FOCUS:pressure-equality-label>> You push down on the small piston with a small force f. That creates a pressure of f divided by a inside the liquid. By Pascal's Law, that same pressure now pushes up on the large piston — across the entire large area A. <<TRACE:pressure-equality-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> The output force on the large piston equals the input force scaled up by the ratio of the large area to the small area — Pascal's transmitted pressure acting over a much bigger surface. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{out}} = f \cdot \frac{A}{a}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:output-force-arrow>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{out}} = \frac{f}{a} \times A = f \cdot \frac{A}{a}|id=eq-2>>The output force on the large piston is that pressure multiplied by the big area. So the output force equals the input force scaled up by the ratio of the areas — A divided by a. Make the big piston a hundred times wider in area and you get a hundred times the force out. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A flask fitted with a piston of cross-sectional area A is filled with liquid. An external force F is applied on the piston. By how much does the pressure increase at a point B located a vertical distance z below the piston?|id=ex-q-1>> Imagine a flask completely filled with an incompressible liquid, and a piston of cross-sectional area A is fitted snugly at the top. We then push down on the piston with an external force F. Now, the pressure just below the piston increases by F divided by A — that's the extra force spread over the piston's cross-sectional area. <<WRITE_STEP:Pressure increase at piston = F / A|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next, consider point B sitting a vertical distance z below the piston. Because the liquid is in hydrostatic equilibrium, the pressure at B must always be rho times g times z more than the pressure at the piston — that depth term accounts for the weight of the liquid column above B. <<WRITE_STEP:Pressure at B = Pressure at piston + (rho × g × z)|id=ex-step-1-2>> The crucial observation is that the liquid is incompressible, so applying the force does not appreciably change z — the distance between the piston and point B stays the same. <<PAUSE:short>> That means the pressure difference rho times g times z between B and the piston remains unchanged. So, since the pressure at the piston increases by F divided by A, and the gap z does not change, the pressure at point B also increases by exactly F divided by A — the same amount. This is Pascal's Law in action: an external pressure change applied anywhere in an enclosed, incompressible liquid is transmitted equally to every point in that liquid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Pressure increase at B = F / A   (same as at the piston, because z is unchanged)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on Pascal's Law — the hydraulic lift. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A hydraulic lift has two vertical cylinders A and B with cross-sectional areas A1 and A2. A force F1 is applied to the narrow piston A. What force F2 is produced on the wider piston B, and is any energy gained?|id=ex-q-1>> We have two cylinders, A and B, connected by a horizontal tube. Cylinder A has cross-sectional area A1, and cylinder B has cross-sectional area A2, where A2 is larger than A1. The load sits on the piston of the larger area A2. A liquid fills the system. We start by finding the pressure increase caused by pushing on piston A. When a force F1 is applied to piston A, by Pascal's Law, the pressure increases everywhere in the liquid by the same amount — that increase is F1 divided by A1. <<WRITE_STEP:Pressure increase = F1 / A1   (transmitted equally throughout the liquid)|id=ex-step-1-1>> This uniform pressure rise is the key: every part of the fluid, including the face of the wider piston B, feels that same extra pressure. Now we find the force this pressure produces on the larger piston B. Force equals pressure times area, so the extra force F2 acting upward on piston B is A2 times the quantity F1 divided by A1. <<WRITE_STEP:F2 = A2 × (F1 / A1)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Because A2 is larger than A1, F2 is larger than F1. In fact, if A2 is much larger than A1, then F2 is much larger than F1 — even a small applied force can raise a heavy load. This is the mechanical advantage of the hydraulic lift. But we must check: is any energy being created here? The answer is no. The work done by F1 equals the work done by F2 — there is no gain in energy. <<WRITE_STEP:Work done by F1 = Work done by F2   (no energy gain)|id=ex-step-1-3>> How does this balance out? Piston A must move downward a larger distance compared to the height that piston B moves up. So you trade a smaller force over a longer distance for a larger force over a shorter distance — exactly like any other simple machine. So to summarise the result: <<WRITE_ANSWER:F2 = A2 × (F1 / A1). Since A2 > A1, the hydraulic lift multiplies force — but work in equals work out, and piston A travels a greater distance than piston B.|id=ex-ans-1>> The force on the large piston F2 equals A2 times F1 divided by A1. The larger the ratio of A2 to A1, the greater the force multiplication. And the energy books always balance — piston A moves down a larger distance than piston B moves up, keeping the total work equal on both sides. <<FOCUS:output-force-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Force multiplication: F_out = f × (A/a)|id=key-2>>This is the power of Pascal's Law in action. The same pressure — transmitted equally everywhere — acts on a huge area and produces a huge force. That's how a small finger lifts a tonne of car. <<POINT:output-force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the elegant core idea is this: a still liquid cannot absorb or hide a pressure change — it must pass it on, perfectly and equally, to every corner of the container. That one fact is Pascal's Law, and it's the reason hydraulic brakes, car lifts, and dentist chairs all work.
