Right now, without you doing anything, a force roughly equal to the weight of a small car is pressing down on your shoulders. Why aren't you crushed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<SECTION:Atmospheric Pressure|id=sec-1>>The answer is that air pushes on you from ALL directions — above, below, left, right — so the forces cancel out. But the pressure itself is very real. <<WRITE_TEXT:Air pushes equally in all directions|id=text-1>>The entire atmosphere, stretching about two hundred kilometers above the earth, has weight, and that weight presses on every surface it touches. <<WRITE_TEXT:More air above = higher pressure below|id=text-2>>Think of it like being at the bottom of a tall stack of blankets. The deeper you are in the stack, the more blankets are above you, and the more you feel pressed down. At the very top of the atmosphere there is nothing above — so pressure there is zero. Down here at ground level, the full column of air above you presses down hard. Now here is the clever part. How do you actually MEASURE something you cannot see? In the sixteen hundreds, a scientist named Torricelli asked exactly that question — and built a device that turns invisible air pressure into a visible height of liquid. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_4:barometer_diagram>> <<SECTION:The Barometer|id=sec-2>>Imagine taking a glass tube about one meter long, sealing one end, filling it completely with mercury, then flipping it upside down into a dish of mercury — keeping the open end submerged. What do you think happens to the mercury inside the tube? <<TRACE:glass-tube>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:mercury-column>> The mercury column FALLS — but only partway. It does not all drain out. It stops at about seventy-six centimeters above the dish surface. <<WRITE_TEXT:Column falls to ~76 cm, then stops|id=text-3>>Above the mercury in the sealed top, a perfect vacuum forms — there is literally nothing there. <<TRACE:mercury-column>> <<FOCUS:atm-pressure-arrow>> Why does it stop there? Look at the dish. The atmosphere is pressing DOWN on the open mercury surface in the dish. That push travels through the liquid and pushes UP inside the tube. <<POINT:atm-pressure-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:column-height-label>> The column can only rise as high as the atmospheric push can support it. The weight of the mercury column pulling it DOWN exactly balances the atmospheric pressure pushing it UP. That balance point — seventy-six centimeters — IS the atmospheric pressure. <<POINT:column-height-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:column-height-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Atmospheric pressure = weight of 76 cm mercury column|id=key-1>>So when someone says 'atmospheric pressure is seventy-six centimeters of mercury', they mean: the atmosphere is strong enough to hold up exactly that height of mercury. No more, no less. <<PAUSE:short>> The pressure at the base of a fluid column equals the fluid's density times g times the height of the column — so the atmospheric pressure outside exactly equals the weight of that seventy-six centimeter mercury column per unit area. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_0 = \rho g h|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:weight-arrow>> Let's write that as an equation. The pressure at the bottom of any fluid column equals the density of the fluid times g times the height. For mercury: P naught equals rho times g times h. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_0 = \rho g h|id=eq-1>>The atmosphere's pressure on the outside pushes up with exactly this value, balancing the weight of the column inside. <<FOCUS:vacuum-space>> Notice what is beautiful here: there is a vacuum at the top of the tube — zero pressure. So the only thing holding the mercury up is the atmosphere pushing from below. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vacuum top → P_top = 0|id=text-4>>If atmospheric pressure increased, the column would rise higher. If it dropped — say on top of a mountain — the column would fall. Here's an example from the chapter. Water is filled in a flask up to a height of twenty centimeters, or zero point two zero meters. The bottom of the flask is circular with a radius of ten centimeters, or zero point one zero meters. Atmospheric pressure is one point zero one times ten to the power five pascals, g is ten meters per second squared, and the density of water is one thousand kilograms per cubic meter. The question asks: what is the force exerted by the water on the bottom of the flask? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Water fills a flask to height h = 0.20 m, circular bottom radius r = 0.10 m. Atmospheric pressure P₀ = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, g = 10 m/s², ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Find force on the bottom.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by finding the pressure at the bottom of the flask. The pressure at the water surface equals atmospheric pressure — that's our starting point. The pressure at the bottom is found using the formula: P equals P0 plus h times rho times g. <<WRITE_STEP:P = P₀ + h·ρ·g|id=ex-step-1-1>> Substituting in, that's one point zero one times ten to the power five pascals, plus zero point two zero meters times one thousand kilograms per cubic meter times ten meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa + (0.20)(1000)(10) Pa|id=ex-step-1-2>> Working through that arithmetic, the second term gives us zero point zero two times ten to the power five pascals. Adding the two terms together, the pressure at the bottom works out to one point zero three times ten to the power five pascals. <<WRITE_STEP:P = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 0.02 × 10⁵ = 1.03 × 10⁵ Pa|id=ex-step-1-3>> Notice how the liquid column adds a small but real contribution on top of atmospheric pressure. Now we need the area of the circular bottom. The area equals pi times r squared. Substituting the radius of zero point one zero meters, that's three point one four times zero point zero one square meters, which gives us zero point zero three one four square meters. <<WRITE_STEP:A = π r² = 3.14 × (0.10)² = 3.14 × 0.01 = 0.0314 m²|id=ex-step-1-4>> Finally, the force on the bottom equals pressure times area. That's one point zero three times ten to the power five pascals multiplied by zero point zero three one four square meters. <<WRITE_STEP:F = P × A = 1.03 × 10⁵ × 0.0314|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<PAUSE:short>> Multiplying those out gives us three thousand two hundred and thirty newtons. <<WRITE_ANSWER:F = 3230 newtons|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example straight from the chapter on atmospheric pressure and barometers. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A barometer shows a mercury column height of seventy-six centimeters. What is the atmospheric pressure in pascals?|id=ex-q-1>> Atmospheric pressure is often expressed as the height of a mercury column. We're told the density of mercury is thirteen point six times ten to the power three kilograms per cubic meter, g is nine point eight meters per second squared, and the height of the mercury column is zero point seven six meters — that's seventy-six centimeters. We use the barometer pressure formula: P naught equals rho times g times h. Plugging in our values — density thirteen point six times ten to the power three kilograms per cubic meter, times g equals nine point eight meters per second squared, times h equals zero point seven six meters. <<WRITE_STEP:P₀ = ρ × g × h = (13.6 × 10³ kg/m³) × (9.8 m/s²) × (0.76 m)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Let's multiply these through. Thirteen point six times ten to the power three, times nine point eight, times zero point seven six gives us approximately one point zero one times ten to the power five. And so the atmospheric pressure works out to one point zero one times ten to the power five pascals. <<WRITE_ANSWER:P₀ = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa = 1 atm|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> This pressure is defined as exactly one atmosphere — written as one atm. So seventy-six centimeters of mercury in a barometer corresponds precisely to the standard definition of one atmosphere of pressure. <<FOCUS:atm-pressure-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Barometer: atmosphere pushes open surface → holds column up|id=key-2>>So the barometer does not suck mercury up — there is nothing sucking. The atmosphere PUSHES the mercury up from below. That is the crucial idea: a barometer measures how hard the atmosphere is pushing. <<POINT:atm-pressure-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Because air is not very dense, atmospheric pressure barely changes between two nearby places at the same altitude — like different spots in the same city. So we can say 'atmospheric pressure is seventy-six centimeters of mercury' for an entire city without worrying about which street you are on.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_5>>
<<FOCUS:fluid-container>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_5:buoyancy_diagram>> Have you ever noticed that lifting a heavy rock underwater feels almost effortless — but the moment you lift it out, it suddenly feels crushing? The water is doing something remarkable. What exactly is it pushing against? <<SECTION:Buoyancy — the upward push of a fluid|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:submerged-body>> Here is our setup. A solid block sitting fully underwater inside a tank of fluid. The fluid is in contact with every face of that block — top, bottom, left, right. <<WRITE_TEXT:Fluid presses on every face of a submerged object|id=text-1>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrows-sides>> The side forces — left and right — push equally hard toward the center. They cancel each other out perfectly. Nothing net happening horizontally. <<POINT:pressure-arrows-sides>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrow-top>> But look at the top and bottom faces. The bottom of the block sits deeper in the fluid. Deeper means higher pressure. So the upward push on the bottom is stronger than the downward push on the top. <<WRITE_TEXT:Deeper → higher pressure → stronger upward push|id=text-2>> <<POINT:pressure-arrow-top>> <<FOCUS:buoyant-force-arrow>> When you add up every tiny force the fluid exerts on the block, all the sideways contributions cancel — and what survives is one single net force pointing straight up. That surviving force is what we call the buoyant force. <<TRACE:buoyant-force-arrow>> Now here is the brilliant question Archimedes answered: how BIG is that upward force? <<WRITE_TEXT:How big is the buoyant force?|id=text-3>> <<POINT:buoyant-force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:displaced-fluid-region>> Imagine scooping the solid block out and pouring fluid back in to fill the exact same shape — the same volume, the same boundary. Now the whole tank is just fluid again. That filled-in region sits perfectly still. It is in equilibrium. <<WRITE_TEXT:Replace body with same-shaped fluid → equilibrium|id=text-4>> <<TRACE:displaced-fluid-region>> The buoyant force B equals the weight of the fluid that was shoved aside — the displaced fluid's mass times g. <<WRITE_EQUATION:B = mg_{\text{displaced fluid}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:weight-displaced-label>> Two forces act on that imaginary plug of fluid: its own weight pulling it down, and the push from all the surrounding fluid. Because it is not moving, those two forces must be exactly equal and opposite. The buoyant force B equals the weight of that plug — the weight of the displaced fluid. <<WRITE_KEY:Buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid|id=key-1>> <<POINT:weight-displaced-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:submerged-body>> And here is the elegant part — the surrounding fluid does not care whether that space is filled with our imaginary plug of fluid OR with the original solid block. The boundary is identical, so the contact forces are identical. The buoyant force on the real block is exactly the same. <<WRITE_TEXT:Same boundary → same contact forces → same B|id=text-5>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> This means Archimedes' principle is not a mysterious new law — it falls straight out of Newton's laws. If the substituted fluid is in balance, the forces on the real object must be the same. <<WRITE_KEY:Archimedes' principle follows from Newton's laws|id=key-2>> <<SECTION:What controls the buoyant force|id=sec-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:displaced-fluid-region>> So what actually controls how large the buoyant force is? Only two things: the density of the fluid, and the volume of the object that is submerged. The material of the object — steel, wood, rubber — is irrelevant. Only the displaced volume matters. <<WRITE_TEXT:B depends on: fluid density × submerged volume × g|id=text-6>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A 700 gram solid cube with edge length 10 centimeters floats in water. How much of the cube's volume is outside the water? Density of water equals 1000 kilograms per cubic meter.|id=ex-q-1>> A solid cube has a mass of seven hundred grams, that's zero point seven kilograms, and each edge is ten centimeters long. It's floating in water, and we want to find how much of that cube sits above the surface. We start by recognising that the cube is in equilibrium — so the buoyant force exactly equals the weight of the cube. And by Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force equals the weight of the water displaced. If a volume V of the cube is submerged, the weight of the displaced water equals V times rho times g, where rho is the density of water. <<WRITE_STEP:Buoyant force = weight of displaced water = V × ρ × g|id=ex-step-1-1>> Setting that equal to the weight of the cube gives us V times rho times g equals zero point seven kilograms times g. <<WRITE_STEP:V × ρ × g = 0.7 kg × g|id=ex-step-1-2>> Notice that g cancels from both sides, which is very convenient. So we get V equals zero point seven kilograms divided by rho, which is zero point seven kilograms divided by one thousand kilograms per cubic meter. <<WRITE_STEP:V = 0.7 kg ÷ 1000 kg/m³ = 7 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 700 cm³|id=ex-step-1-3>> That works out to seven times ten to the power of negative four cubic meters, which is the same as seven hundred cubic centimeters. So seven hundred cubic centimeters of the cube is submerged underwater. Now let's find the total volume of the cube. The edge length is ten centimeters, so the total volume is ten cubed, which equals one thousand cubic centimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:Total volume = 10³ = 1000 cm³|id=ex-step-1-4>> The volume outside the water is simply the total volume minus the submerged volume — that's one thousand minus seven hundred, which equals three hundred cubic centimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:Volume outside water = 1000 − 700 = 300 cm³|id=ex-step-1-5>> And there's our answer. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Volume outside water = 300 cubic centimeters|id=ex-ans-1>> Three hundred cubic centimeters of the cube sits above the water surface. That's thirty percent of the cube peeking out — which makes sense, since the cube's effective density is seven hundred kilograms per cubic meter, less than water's one thousand kilograms per cubic meter, so it floats with just the right fraction submerged to balance its weight. That is why a massive steel ship floats. Its hull is shaped to displace a huge volume of water — enough that the weight of all that displaced water exceeds the ship's own weight. The ocean pushes back harder than gravity pulls down. <<POINT:buoyant-force-arrow>> <<FOCUS:buoyant-force-arrow>> So the one thing to lock in: the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid — nothing more, nothing less. Bigger displaced volume, bigger buoyant force. Denser fluid, bigger buoyant force. That single idea explains floating, sinking, and everything in between. <<WRITE_KEY:B = weight of displaced fluid — the one rule for floating and sinking|id=key-3>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_6>>
<<FOCUS:elevator-box>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_6:elevator_fluid>> Here's a strange one — if you're in an elevator holding a glass of water, and the elevator suddenly shoots upward, the water feels heavier. But if the elevator cable snaps and you're in free fall, the water feels weightless. How can the same liquid in the same glass 'weigh' something completely different? <<FOCUS:fluid-cylinder>> <<SECTION:Fluid in an Accelerating Elevator|id=sec-1>>Let's build the picture carefully. We've got a beaker of liquid riding in an elevator accelerating upward at a zero. Inside that liquid, pick any two points — call them A and B — with B sitting directly above A by a vertical height z. <<POINT:fluid-cylinder>> <<POINT:fluid-cylinder>> Imagine carving out a tiny vertical cylinder of liquid between A and B. Three forces act on it vertically: pressure from below pushing up, pressure from above pushing down, and gravity pulling it down. <<TRACE:fluid-cylinder>> <<POINT:fluid-cylinder>> <<POINT:fluid-cylinder>> <<POINT:fluid-cylinder>> <<FOCUS:arrow-P1>> <<FOCUS:arrow-P1>> <<FOCUS:arrow-P1>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Forces on fluid cylinder: P1·S up, P2·S down, mg down|id=text-1>>The upward push is P one times S — that's the pressure at A multiplied by the cross-sectional area. The downward pushes are P two times S from above, plus the weight m g of the fluid itself. <<FOCUS:arrow-accel>> Now here's the key question: this cylinder isn't sitting still — it's accelerating upward at a zero along with the whole elevator. So according to Newton's second law, the NET upward force on it must equal m times a zero, not zero. How does that change the pressure difference? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:height-z>> <<WRITE_STEP:P1·S − P2·S − mg = m·a0|id=step-1>>Newton's second law says: P one S minus P two S minus m g equals m times a zero. Rearranging, the pressure difference P one minus P two equals rho times the quantity g plus a zero, all times z — where rho is the density of the liquid. <<PAUSE:short>> The net upward force must drive the acceleration, so the pressure difference picks up an extra a zero term alongside g — giving us an effective gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_1 - P_2 = \rho(g + a_0)z|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:fluid-cylinder>> <<WRITE_KEY:P1 − P2 = ρ(g + a₀)z — effective gravity replaces g|id=key-1>>Notice what happened: gravity g just got replaced by an 'effective gravity' of g plus a zero. The fluid acts as though gravity itself got stronger. That's why your water feels heavier in an upward-accelerating elevator. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:elevator-box>> <<SECTION:Buoyant Force in an Accelerating Fluid|id=sec-2>>Now let's think about buoyancy. You already know from Archimedes' principle that the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid — rho times V times g. But that was for a stationary fluid. <<FOCUS:fluid-cylinder>> In the accelerating elevator, every pressure force on a submerged object scales with that same effective gravity g plus a zero. So the net upward pressure force — the buoyant force — becomes rho times V times the quantity g plus a zero. <<PAUSE:short>> Since every pressure in the fluid now scales with effective gravity, the buoyant force formula simply replaces g with g plus a zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{buoyant}} = \rho V (g + a_0)|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A beaker of liquid is in an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Points A and B are in the liquid, with B at vertical height z above A. The liquid has density rho. Find the pressure difference P1 minus P2 between A and B.|id=ex-q-1>> Suppose a beaker contains some liquid placed in an elevator going up with an acceleration a0. We have two points, A and B, inside the liquid, where B is at a vertical height z above A. The pressure at A is P1 and the pressure at B is P2, and the liquid has density rho. We isolate a small vertical cylinder of liquid with a horizontal cross-sectional area S at each face — one face at A, one face at B. Now let's list the three vertical forces acting on this cylinder of liquid. <<WRITE_STEP:Forces on the cylinder (vertical direction):|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:(a) P1 times S — upward, from liquid below|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:(b) P2 times S — downward, from liquid above|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:(c) weight = S times z times rho times g — downward|id=ex-step-1-4>> First, P1 times S acts upward due to the liquid below the cylinder. Second, P2 times S acts downward due to the liquid above it. And third, the weight of the liquid in the cylinder acts downward — that weight equals the volume S times z, multiplied by density rho, multiplied by g. Now, the entire elevator — and therefore this cylinder of liquid — is accelerating upward with acceleration a0. So we apply Newton's second law in the vertical direction. The net upward force equals mass times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:Newton's second law (upward positive):|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<WRITE_STEP:P1·S − P2·S − S·z·rho·g = S·z·rho·a0|id=ex-step-1-6>> The left-hand side has P1 times S upward, minus P2 times S downward, minus the weight S times z times rho times g downward. The right-hand side is the mass S times z times rho, multiplied by a0. Let's rearrange. We bring the weight term to the right-hand side, so the right side becomes mass times g plus mass times a0. Then we factor out S times z times rho on the right, and divide both sides by S. <<WRITE_STEP:(P1 − P2)·S = S·z·rho·g + S·z·rho·a0|id=ex-step-1-7>> <<WRITE_STEP:P1 − P2 = rho·(g + a0)·z|id=ex-step-1-8>> <<PAUSE:short>> Dividing through by S, we get P1 minus P2 equals rho times the quantity g plus a0, times z. Notice this is exactly like the static pressure formula, except gravity g has been effectively replaced by g plus a0 — the upward acceleration adds to gravity. And so the final result is: <<WRITE_ANSWER:P1 − P2 = rho × (g + a0) × z|id=ex-ans-1>> The pressure difference between point A and point B, where B is a vertical height z above A, is rho times the quantity g plus a0, times z. When the elevator accelerates upward, the effective gravity increases from g to g plus a0, and the pressure difference between any two vertical points in the liquid increases accordingly. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A body is fully submerged in a liquid of density rho, inside an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Find the buoyant force B on the body.|id=ex-q-1>> Suppose a body is fully submerged in a liquid of density rho — that's our liquid — and the elevator is going up with an upward acceleration a0. We want to find the buoyant force B acting on the body. The key idea is the substitution trick. We mentally replace the submerged body with the same volume of liquid — that is, we fill that space with the surrounding liquid. Since the whole liquid is now a homogeneous mass, this substituted portion is at rest relative to the rest of the liquid, so it accelerates upward at a0 together with everything else. <<WRITE_STEP:Substituted liquid: mass m = mass of displaced liquid, accelerating upward at a0|id=ex-step-1-1>> The substituted liquid has mass m equal to the mass of the displaced liquid, and it is moving upward with the same acceleration a0. Now let's identify the two forces acting on the substituted liquid. <<WRITE_STEP:Forces on substituted liquid: (a) Buoyant force B — upward, (b) Weight mg — downward|id=ex-step-1-2>> First, there is the buoyant force B acting upward, supplied by the surrounding liquid. Second, there is the weight m times g acting downward. These are the only two forces — there is no contact force from a solid body anymore, because we replaced that body with liquid. We apply Newton's second law to the substituted liquid. The net upward force equals m times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:Newton's second law → B − mg = m times a0|id=ex-step-1-3>> So B minus m times g equals m times a0. Rearranging, we bring m times g to the right-hand side. <<WRITE_STEP:Rearranging → B = m times g + m times a0 = m times (g + a0)|id=ex-step-1-4>> That gives us B equals m times g plus m times a0, which we factor as m times the quantity g plus a0. And there is the answer. <<WRITE_ANSWER:B = m(g + a0), where m is the mass of the displaced liquid|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> The buoyant force is B equals m times the quantity g plus a0, where m is the mass of the displaced liquid. Notice that the effective gravitational pull has been replaced by g plus a0 — so when the elevator accelerates upward, buoyancy becomes stronger than it would be at rest. The faster the upward acceleration a0, the greater the buoyant force on any submerged object. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A beaker of liquid accelerates horizontally with acceleration a0. Points A and B are at the same horizontal level, separated by distance l along the direction of acceleration. The liquid has density rho. Find the tilt angle theta of the free surface.|id=ex-q-2>> We have a beaker accelerating horizontally with acceleration a0. Points A and B sit at the same horizontal level, separated by distance l along the direction of that acceleration. The pressure at A is P1 and the pressure at B is P2, and the density of the liquid is rho. Our goal is to find how steeply the free surface tilts. We start by applying Newton's second law to a small horizontal cylinder of liquid connecting A to B. The liquid on the left pushes with force P1 times delta S toward the right, and the liquid on the right pushes back with P2 times delta S toward the left. The mass of liquid in that cylinder is delta S times l times rho. Setting net force equal to mass times acceleration we get: P1 times delta S minus P2 times delta S equals delta S times l times rho times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:(P1 − P2)ΔS = (ΔS) · l · ρ · a0|id=ex-step-2-1>> Dividing both sides by delta S, this simplifies beautifully: P1 minus P2 equals l times rho times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 − P2 = l · ρ · a0|id=ex-step-2-2>> So even though A and B are at the same horizontal level, there IS a pressure difference between them whenever the liquid accelerates horizontally. Now we bring in the depth expressions. Because there is no vertical acceleration, the usual hydrostatic rule still holds vertically. So the pressure at A is P0 plus h1 times rho times g, and the pressure at B is P0 plus h2 times rho times g, where h1 and h2 are the depths of A and B below the free surface. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 = P0 + h1·ρ·g,   P2 = P0 + h2·ρ·g|id=ex-step-2-3>> We substitute these into our earlier result P1 minus P2 equals l times rho times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:(P0 + h1·ρ·g) − (P0 + h2·ρ·g) = l·ρ·a0|id=ex-step-2-4>> The atmospheric pressure P0 cancels on both sides, and rho cancels too, leaving us with: h1 times g minus h2 times g equals l times a0. Dividing both sides by l times g gives us the slope of the free surface. <<WRITE_STEP:(h1 − h2) / l = a0 / g|id=ex-step-2-5>> Now look at what the left-hand side means geometrically: h1 minus h2 is the vertical rise across the horizontal distance l. That ratio is exactly the tangent of the angle theta that the free surface makes with the horizontal. <<WRITE_STEP:tan θ = (h1 − h2) / l = a0 / g|id=ex-step-2-6>> So the free surface tilts at an angle whose tangent equals a0 divided by g. <<WRITE_ANSWER:tan θ = a0 / g  (theta = tilt angle of the free surface)|id=ex-ans-2>> The faster the beaker accelerates, the steeper the tilt — and notice it doesn't depend on the density of the liquid or the separation l at all. <<WRITE_KEY:Buoyant force = ρV(g + a₀) in accelerating fluid|id=key-2>>That means in an upward-accelerating elevator, objects feel MORE buoyancy — they float more easily. And in free fall, a zero equals minus g, so g plus a zero equals zero, and the buoyant force vanishes entirely. That's your weightless water. <<POINT:arrow-accel>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:height-z>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Free fall: a₀ = −g → buoyancy = 0|id=text-2>>So to tie it together: whether we're talking about pressure difference between two points or the buoyant force on a submerged body, the rule is the same — swap out g for the effective gravity g plus a zero. The fluid 'forgets' that it's in an elevator; it just responds to whatever net downward pull it feels.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_7>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_7:waterfall_complexity>> Every single water droplet in a waterfall perfectly obeys Newton's laws — force equals mass times acceleration, every particle, every moment. So why can't we predict where any one of them will land? <<TRACE:droplet-crowd>> <<FOCUS:single-droplet>> <<SECTION:Fluids and Newton's Laws|id=sec-1>>Let's zoom in. Take just one droplet out of that waterfall. It has a mass, gravity pulls it down, and we can write every force acting on it. Newton's laws are crystal clear here. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Each droplet: F = ma, every moment|id=text-1>>The same physics you used to calculate a ball rolling down a ramp applies right here — to this one droplet. Simple. Clean. Predictable. <<POINT:force-arrow>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now put all the droplets back together. <<TRACE:droplet-crowd>> <<FOCUS:interaction-lines>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Billions of droplets → billions of interactions|id=text-2>>Each one is bumping into its neighbours, being pushed sideways, losing speed here, gaining it there. The interactions between particles explode in number. <<TRACE:interaction-lines>> Here's the real question: if every particle is following simple, known laws — why is it so impossibly hard to work out what even one droplet will do? <<POINT:droplet-crowd>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:interaction-lines>> <<WRITE_KEY:Complexity comes from interactions, not from the rules|id=key-1>>The answer is that complexity doesn't come from the rules — it comes from the interactions. Billions of particles, each affecting every neighbour, every instant. The maths doesn't break down; it just becomes astronomically large. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> It's the same story with smoke rising from a fire. Every smoke particle obeys Newton's second law — you could write the equation for it right now. But watch smoke curl and twist and loop back on itself — that's the same equations playing out across millions of particles at once. <<PAUSE:short>> Or think about clouds drifting across the sky. Each tiny water droplet and air molecule is following the same simple rule: net force equals mass times acceleration. The grand, sweeping motion of the whole cloud emerges from uncountable tiny interactions. <<WRITE_KEY:Fluid flow: simple laws, staggering complexity|id=key-2>>So here is the big idea to hold onto: fluid mechanics is NOT about new physics. It is Newton's old laws, applied to so many particles at once that prediction becomes the challenge — not the principles. <<PAUSE:short>> This is why fluid flow is one of the richest, most beautiful — and most difficult — areas of classical mechanics. And the first step to taming it is to classify what kinds of flow are even possible. That's exactly where we go next.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_8>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Why does water from a tap sometimes flow in a perfectly smooth, glassy ribbon — and other times come out in a wild, splashing mess, even though it's the same tap? The answer is one of the most elegant ideas in fluid physics. <<FOCUS:point-A>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_8:flow_comparison>> <<SECTION:Steady Flow|id=sec-1>>Imagine liquid moving slowly through a pipe. Pick any single point inside — let's call it point A. Particle after particle arrives at A. Because the flow is slow and calm, every single one of them arrives with the same speed, travelling in the same direction. It doesn't matter when they arrive — the condition at A is always identical. <<POINT:streamline-1>> <<TRACE:streamline-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:point-B>> Now follow one of those particles forward — it travels from A to point B along a specific curved path. <<TRACE:point-B>> Here is the key insight: because every particle arrives at A in exactly the same state, every particle takes that exact same path to B. The path is shared. This shared path is called a streamline. <<WRITE_KEY:Steady flow → every particle through A follows the same streamline|id=key-1>> <<TRACE:streamline-1>> <<POINT:streamline-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> And it's not just one streamline — the whole pipe is filled with these neat, parallel lanes. Different particles travel on different streamlines, but the lanes never cross. <<WRITE_TEXT:Streamlines never cross each other|id=text-1>> <<TRACE:streamline-2>> <<TRACE:streamline-2>> <<FOCUS:streamline-3>> This is called steady flow — or streamline flow. The word 'steady' here has a precise meaning: the velocity at every fixed point in the fluid stays the same over time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Steady flow = velocity at each point constant in time|id=text-2>> Now here's a question worth sitting with: what do you think happens if we push the liquid through the pipe much faster — really crank up the speed? Does the flow stay nice and orderly? <<POINT:turbulent-region>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:turbulent-region>> <<SECTION:Turbulent Flow|id=sec-2>>It breaks down completely. Once the speed crosses a critical threshold, the flow becomes turbulent — chaotic, swirling, unpredictable. <<TRACE:turbulent-region>> <<FOCUS:turbulent-point-C>> Look at point C inside the turbulent region. Two different particles passing through C at different moments don't just have slightly different speeds — they can be heading in completely different directions. The streamline picture falls apart entirely. <<WRITE_KEY:Turbulent flow → velocity at same point changes erratically|id=key-2>> <<POINT:turbulent-point-C>> <<PAUSE:short>> This is exactly what you see in a fast-flowing river or the churning white water at the base of a waterfall — every bit of water seems to have a mind of its own, because the flow condition at every point is constantly changing. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So back to the tap: slow flow means the water at the spout exit is always in the same state, so every drop follows the same glassy path — steady flow. Turn the tap wide open, speed shoots up, and the condition at the exit flickers erratically — turbulent flow. Same tap, same water, completely different world. <<WRITE_TEXT:Slow → steady (streamline). Fast → turbulent|id=text-3>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_9>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_9:fluid_assumptions>> When you stir water in a bucket, every little bit of water spins around. But rivers can flow smoothly for kilometres without a single whirlpool. What's the difference — and why does it matter so much to engineers? <<TRACE:bucket-vortex>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:The Three Magic Assumptions|id=sec-1>>To make the maths of flowing fluids manageable, physicists zero in on a special kind of fluid — one that satisfies three clean assumptions. Let's build each one from scratch. <<FOCUS:density-dots-uniform>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Assumption 1 — Incompressible: density same everywhere, always|id=text-1>>First: incompressibility. Push water as hard as you like — it refuses to squish. Its density stays the same at every point and at every moment. Liquids are almost always like this. <<FOCUS:viscous-layers>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Assumption 2 — Nonviscous: no internal friction|id=text-2>>Second: nonviscosity. Real fluids have layers that slide over each other, and that sliding creates internal friction — a bit like rubbing your hands together. Energy gets lost as heat. <<FOCUS:nonviscous-layers>> A nonviscous fluid simply ignores that friction. One layer glides past the next with zero resistance — no energy wasted. Water and air, at everyday speeds, are remarkably close to this ideal. <<FOCUS:irrotational-particle>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Assumption 3 — Irrotational: no particle spins about its own axis|id=text-3>>Third — and this is the trickiest one. Irrotational. Here's the question: can a fluid particle travel along a curved path WITHOUT spinning about its own centre? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:irrotational-particle>> Absolutely yes. Think of a car going around a roundabout — the car follows a curved road, but the car itself isn't rolling sideways. Irrotational means each tiny blob of fluid has zero net rotation about its own axis, even as the whole flow curves. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:bucket-vortex>> <<WRITE_KEY:Irrotational ≠ straight-line flow. It means no individual particle self-spins.|id=key-1>>Compare it to rotational flow — stir a bucket and you create a vortex. Every particle of water is literally spinning about a central axis. That's rotational flow, and it makes the equations far harder. <<TRACE:bucket-vortex>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:river-streamlines>> A smooth river, away from eddies, is the opposite: the water moves forward, follows bends, but no particle tumbles about itself. That's irrotational flow in the real world. <<TRACE:river-streamlines>> So now put all three together. Incompressible: density is locked. Nonviscous: no energy lost to friction. Irrotational: no particle self-spins. A fluid that ticks all three boxes is called an ideal fluid. <<POINT:nonviscous-layers>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ideal fluid = incompressible + nonviscous + irrotational → no energy loss, maths stays clean.|id=key-2>>Here's why this matters: an ideal fluid flowing through any pipe or channel conserves all of its mechanical energy. Nothing leaks away. That single fact unlocks the beautiful equations we'll use from here on. <<POINT:density-dots-uniform>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Is the ideal fluid real? Not perfectly — no fluid is truly frictionless. But water, air, and many gases behave close enough that the ideal-fluid predictions match experiments to within a few percent. That's why every engineer learns this model first. So the next time you see water flowing calmly in a channel — no whirlpools, no churning — you're looking at something very close to our ideal fluid: incompressible, nonviscous, and irrotational. Those three words are the passport to all the elegant fluid physics ahead. <<TRACE:river-streamlines>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_10>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Squeeze the end of a garden hose with your thumb — the water doesn't slow down, it shoots out faster. Why does making the opening smaller speed the water up? The answer is hiding in one of the most elegant ideas in all of fluid mechanics. <<FOCUS:wide-section>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_10:continuity_tube>> <<SECTION:Tubes of Flow|id=sec-1>>Think of a flowing fluid — water in a pipe, blood in a vein — as a bundle of invisible tubes, each carrying its own private stream. <<WRITE_TEXT:Fluid in one tube never mixes with fluid in another|id=text-1>>The fluid in one tube never mixes with fluid in any neighbouring tube. Each stream stays in its own lane. <<FOCUS:wide-section>> Now here is the key constraint: fluid can't pile up inside the tube, and it can't vanish. <<WRITE_KEY:Mass in = Mass out (conservation of mass)|id=key-1>>Whatever mass enters one end of a tube must come out the other end in the same time. This is just conservation of mass. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:cylinder-A>> Look at the wide end of the tube — cross section A. The fluid here is moving with speed v one. In a short time delta t, how far does it travel? A distance of v one times delta t. <<TRACE:cylinder-A>> <<FOCUS:cylinder-A>> That slab of fluid — with face area A one and length v one delta t — is a cylinder. Its volume is A one times v one times delta t. That is the volume that enters the tube every delta t seconds through the wide end. <<FOCUS:cylinder-B>> Now look at the narrow end — cross section B. The same argument applies: the volume leaving the tube there every delta t seconds is A two times v two times delta t. <<TRACE:cylinder-B>> <<FOCUS:cross-section-B>> <<SECTION:Why Speed Must Change|id=sec-2>>Here is the question: if A two is smaller than A one, what has to happen to v two to make sure the same volume flows out per second as flows in? <<POINT:cross-section-B>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:cylinder-B>> Because the fluid is incompressible, the two volumes must be equal. <<WRITE_STEP:A₁v₁Δt = A₂v₂Δt|id=step-1>>So A one times v one times delta t equals A two times v two times delta t. The delta t cancels from both sides. <<POINT:cylinder-B>> The volume entering at A every second must equal the volume leaving at B every second — so area times speed on the left equals area times speed on the right. <<WRITE_EQUATION:A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:cross-section-A>> <<WRITE_KEY:A₁v₁ = A₂v₂  (Equation of Continuity)|id=key-2>>We are left with A one times v one equals A two times v two. This is the equation of continuity. Area times speed is the same at every cross section of the tube. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:velocity-arrow-B>> Read it directly from the picture: where the tube is narrow, A two is small, so v two must be large to keep the product constant. Where the tube is wide, A one is large, so v one is small. A smaller opening forces higher speed. That is why the hose squirt works. <<POINT:velocity-arrow-B>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. A liquid is being pushed out of a tube by pressing a piston. The area of cross section of the piston is one point zero square centimeters, and the area of the tube at the outlet is twenty square millimeters. The piston is pushed at a speed of two centimeters per second. We need to find the speed of the outgoing liquid. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Piston area A1 = 1.0 cm², outlet area A2 = 20 mm², piston speed v1 = 2 cm/s. Find v2.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by applying the equation of continuity, which tells us that A one times v one equals A two times v two. Let's write that down and plug in the known values straight away. <<WRITE_STEP:A₁v₁ = A₂v₂|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:(1.0 cm²)(2 cm/s) = (20 mm²) × v₂|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now, notice that A one is in square centimeters while A two is in square millimeters — we can't divide them directly. We need a consistent unit. The key conversion here is that one point zero square centimeter equals one hundred square millimeters. So we replace A one with one hundred square millimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:v₂ = (1.0 cm² / 20 mm²) × 2 cm/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:v₂ = (100 mm² / 20 mm²) × 2 cm/s|id=ex-step-1-4>> One hundred divided by twenty gives us five, and five times two is ten. So the speed of the outgoing liquid is ten centimeters per second. Because the outlet area is smaller than the piston area, the fluid speeds up — exactly what the equation of continuity predicts. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:v₂ = 10 cm/s|id=ex-ans-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Av = constant everywhere in tube|id=text-2>>So the quantity A times v — called the volume flow rate — stays constant all the way along the tube. It doesn't matter how many times the tube bends or changes shape. <<TRACE:narrow-section>> And never forget where this equation comes from: it is not a new law of physics. It is conservation of mass wearing fluid-mechanics clothing. If mass is conserved and the fluid cannot be compressed, the product A times v has no choice but to stay constant. <<POINT:cross-section-A>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_11>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's something that will mess with your head: the faster a fluid flows, the LOWER its pressure. Speed up — pressure drops. Slow down — pressure rises. That feels completely backwards. But it's the reason aeroplanes fly, and it's all hiding inside one beautiful equation. <<FOCUS:pipe-wide-section>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_11:bernoulli_pipe>> <<SECTION:Setup — the pipe|id=sec-1>>You already know the equation of continuity: when a pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up to keep the same volume flowing every second. Now let's ask a deeper question — what happens to the PRESSURE when that happens? <<FOCUS:pipe-wide-section>> Picture this pipe — wide and low on the left, narrow and high on the right. Fluid is flowing steadily; it's incompressible, so nothing squishes; and there's no friction slowing it down. At the wide end, call the area A one, the speed v one, the pressure P one, and the height h one. <<POINT:pipe-wide-section>> <<FOCUS:pipe-narrow-section>> At the narrow end: area A two, speed v two, pressure P two, height h two. <<POINT:pipe-narrow-section>> <<FOCUS:fluid-element-A>> <<SECTION:Work done by pressure forces|id=sec-2>>Now let's track a small chunk of fluid — mass delta m — as it shifts from the wide section to the narrow one. Two pressure forces do work on it: the pressure behind it at the inlet PUSHES it forward, and the pressure ahead at the outlet PUSHES BACK. <<TRACE:fluid-element-A>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrow-P1>> The force at the inlet is P one times A one, and it pushes the chunk through a small distance v one times delta t. So the work done BY the inlet pressure is P one times A one times v one times delta t. <<POINT:pressure-arrow-P1>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrow-P2>> At the outlet, the pressure P two pushes BACK on the chunk over distance v two times delta t — that's negative work: minus P two times A two times v two times delta t. <<WRITE_STEP:Net work = (P1 − P2) × Δm/ρ|id=step-1>> <<POINT:pressure-arrow-P2>> <<FOCUS:fluid-element-B>> <<SECTION:Energy changes|id=sec-3>>By continuity, A one v one equals A two v two, so the volumes are equal and the mass delta m is the same at both ends. The net work by pressure then simplifies to the pressure DIFFERENCE times delta m divided by rho — that's the energy the pressure forces put in. Now, where does that energy GO? The work-energy theorem says it goes into two places: the change in kinetic energy of the chunk, and the change in its gravitational potential energy as it climbs from h one to h two. <<WRITE_STEP:W_pressure = ΔKE + ΔPE|id=step-2>> <<POINT:height-h2>> <<POINT:height-h2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:ΔKE = ½Δm(v₂² − v₁²), ΔPE = Δmg(h₂ − h₁)|id=step-3>>The kinetic energy change is one-half delta m times open bracket v two squared minus v one squared close bracket. The potential energy change is delta m times g times open bracket h two minus h one close bracket. Setting pressure work equal to the sum of these two, and dividing through by the volume delta m over rho, every term becomes energy per unit volume. <<PAUSE:short>> Each term is energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy — and their sum never changes along the flow. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> And when we rearrange, everything from side one equals everything from side two: P one plus one-half rho v one squared plus rho g h one equals P two plus one-half rho v two squared plus rho g h two. <<WRITE_KEY:P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> We can write this more compactly: at any point in the fluid, pressure plus one-half rho v squared plus rho g h equals the same constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}|id=eq-2|boxed>> That's Bernoulli's equation — and notice what it IS: it's the work-energy theorem wearing fluid-mechanics clothes. Each term is energy per unit volume. Pressure energy, kinetic energy, potential energy — they shift between each other, but their SUM stays constant. <<POINT:pipe-narrow-section>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A liquid of density one thousand two hundred kilograms per cubic meter flows steadily through a tube. The cross-sectional area at point A is one point zero square centimeters, and at point B it is twenty square millimeters. Points A and B are at the same horizontal height. The speed at A is ten centimeters per second. Find the difference in pressures at A and B.|id=ex-q-1>> We have a liquid of density one thousand two hundred kilograms per cubic meter, the cross-sectional area at A is one point zero square centimeters, and the cross-sectional area at B is twenty square millimeters. Points A and B are at the same horizontal height, so h one equals h two, and the speed of the liquid at A is ten centimeters per second. Our goal is to find the pressure difference P one minus P two. We start with the continuity equation to find the speed at B, because Bernoulli's equation will need both speeds. The continuity equation says A one times v one equals A two times v two. <<WRITE_STEP:Continuity: A1·v1 = A2·v2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Substituting in our values, one point zero square centimeters times ten centimeters per second equals twenty square millimeters times v two. <<WRITE_STEP:(1.0 cm²)(10 cm/s) = (20 mm²) · v2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Since one point zero square centimeters equals one hundred square millimeters, we get v two equals one hundred square millimeters times ten centimeters per second, all divided by twenty square millimeters. <<PAUSE:short>> That gives us v two equals fifty centimeters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:v2 = (100 mm² × 10 cm/s) ÷ 20 mm² = 50 cm/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> So the speed at B found from the continuity equation is fifty centimeters per second. Now we apply Bernoulli's equation. The full form is P one plus rho g h one plus one half rho v one squared equals P two plus rho g h two plus one half rho v two squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 + ρgh1 + ½ρv1² = P2 + ρgh2 + ½ρv2²|id=ex-step-1-4>> Because points A and B are at the same horizontal height, h one equals h two, so those gravity terms cancel. Rearranging, we get P one minus P two equals one half rho v two squared minus one half rho v one squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Since h1 = h2 → P1 − P2 = ½ρ(v2² − v1²)|id=ex-step-1-5>> Let's now substitute the numbers. v two squared is fifty centimeters per second squared, which is two thousand five hundred square centimeters per second squared. And v one squared is ten centimeters per second squared, which is one hundred square centimeters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:v2² = 2500 cm²/s²,  v1² = 100 cm²/s²|id=ex-step-1-6>> So P one minus P two equals one half times one thousand two hundred kilograms per cubic meter times the quantity two thousand five hundred minus one hundred square centimeters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 − P2 = ½ × 1200 kg/m³ × (2500 − 100) cm²/s²|id=ex-step-1-7>> That simplifies to six hundred kilograms per cubic meter times two thousand four hundred square centimeters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:= 600 kg/m³ × 2400 cm²/s²|id=ex-step-1-8>> Converting square centimeters per second squared to SI units and multiplying through, the pressure difference P one minus P two equals one hundred forty-four pascals. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:P1 − P2 = 144 pascals|id=ex-ans-1>> So the liquid at the narrower point B is moving faster — fifty centimeters per second compared to ten centimeters per second at A — and as Bernoulli's equation tells us, that higher speed comes with a lower pressure, giving us a pressure difference of one hundred forty-four pascals. <<FOCUS:pipe-narrow-section>> <<SECTION:The paradox resolved|id=sec-4>>So now — back to the paradox from the start. Imagine a HORIZONTAL pipe: h one equals h two, so the height terms cancel. The equation becomes P one plus one-half rho v one squared equals P two plus one-half rho v two squared. If the pipe narrows and v two is bigger than v one — what must happen to P two? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Exactly — P two must be SMALLER. The kinetic energy term one-half rho v squared grew because the fluid sped up, so the pressure term P has to SHRINK to keep the total constant. <<WRITE_KEY:Faster flow → lower pressure|id=key-2>>Speed up, pressure drops. That's not backwards — it's energy conservation in action. <<POINT:pressure-arrow-P2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_12>>
<<FOCUS:tank-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_12:efflux_tank>> If you poke a hole near the bottom of a water tank, how fast does the water shoot out? Here's the wild part — the answer is the exact same speed a ball would reach if you simply dropped it from the height of the water surface. Let's see why. <<SECTION:Setting Up the Tank|id=sec-1>>Here's our setup. A tall tank, open at the top, with a small hole near the bottom. The water surface is at a height h above the hole. We call the top surface point one and the hole point two. <<TRACE:tank-body>> <<POINT:tank-body>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Point 1: top surface (open to air)|id=text-1>>Now, both the top surface and the hole are open to the atmosphere, so the pressure at both points is exactly atmospheric pressure. Those two pressure terms cancel out of Bernoulli's equation straight away. <<POINT:top-surface>> <<POINT:top-surface>> <<FOCUS:v1-arrow>> The tank is much, much wider than the hole. By the continuity equation — area times speed is constant — the top surface crawls downward almost imperceptibly compared to the jet at the hole. So we can set v one to essentially zero. <<POINT:v1-arrow>> <<FOCUS:height-h-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:v1 ≈ 0 since tank area >> hole area|id=text-2>>That leaves only two terms in Bernoulli's equation: the potential energy term rho g h on the left, and the kinetic energy term one half rho v two squared on the right. So think about what Bernoulli is telling us: all that height — all that stored gravitational energy per unit volume — gets converted entirely into kinetic energy at the hole. The fluid trades altitude for speed, one-for-one. <<TRACE:height-h-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> All the gravitational potential energy per unit volume, rho g h, converts completely into kinetic energy one half rho v two squared. Solving for v two gives us the efflux speed. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v_2 = \sqrt{2gh}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:v2-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:ρgh = ½ρv₂² → v₂ = √(2gh)|id=step-1>>And when you solve for v two, you get v two equals the square root of two g h. No tank width. No water density. Just the height. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:freefall-path>> Now here's the question that makes this unforgettable: does that formula look familiar to you? Think back to kinematics — what speed does a ball reach after falling freely through a height h? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torricelli's Theorem: v = √(2gh) — same as free fall!|id=key-1>>Exactly the same answer — v equals the square root of two g h. A ball in free fall and water shooting from a hole reach identical speeds over the same vertical drop. This beautiful result is called Torricelli's theorem. <<TRACE:freefall-path>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Hydrostatics as a Special Case|id=sec-2>>Before we move on, here's an elegant sanity check: what if the fluid isn't moving at all? Set both v one and v two to zero in Bernoulli's equation. <<WRITE_STEP:v=0 everywhere → P1 + ρgh1 = P2 + ρgh2|id=step-2>>The kinetic energy terms vanish, and you're left with P one plus rho g h one equals P two plus rho g h two. Rearranging: the pressure difference equals rho g times the difference in height. That's exactly the hydrostatics result you already know. <<PAUSE:short>> When fluid speed is zero everywhere, the kinetic terms drop out of Bernoulli's equation and we recover the familiar hydrostatics pressure-depth relationship. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_1 - P_2 = \rho g (h_2 - h_1)|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A water tank sits on top of a building. With what speed does water come out of a tap six point zero meters below the water level in the tank? Assume steady flow, and that the pressure above the water level equals atmospheric pressure.|id=ex-q-1>> A water tank is constructed on top of a building. The tap is six point zero meters below the water surface. We're told the flow is steady, and that the pressure above the water level is equal to the atmospheric pressure — so Torricelli's theorem applies directly. Torricelli's theorem tells us the exit speed is the same as the speed an object would reach falling freely through the same height h. The formula is v equals the square root of two times g times h. <<WRITE_STEP:v = √(2 × g × h)|id=ex-step-1-1>> We substitute g equals nine point eight meters per second squared and h equals six point zero meters. <<WRITE_STEP:v = √(2 × 9.8 m/s² × 6.0 m)|id=ex-step-1-2>> That gives us the square root of one hundred seventeen point six meters squared per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:v = √(117.6 m²/s²)|id=ex-step-1-3>> Taking the square root, we get approximately eleven meters per second. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:v ≈ 11 m/s (approximately eleven meters per second)|id=ex-ans-1>> So the water shoots out of that tap at approximately eleven meters per second — exactly what you'd expect from a free-fall drop of six meters, which is a neat way to think about it. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Water flows through a horizontal tube. The pressure difference between points A and B is six hundred newtons per meter squared. The cross-sectional area at A is thirty centimeters squared and at B is fifteen centimeters squared. Find the rate of flow of water. (Density of water = one thousand kilograms per meter cubed.)|id=ex-q-1>> Water is flowing through a horizontal tube — so there's no height difference to worry about — and we're told the pressure drops by six hundred newtons per meter squared between the wider section A and the narrower section B. We want to find how much water, in volume per second, is passing through. We start with the continuity equation. Because the tube is horizontal and water is incompressible, the flow rate is the same everywhere, so area times velocity is constant. The cross-sectional area at A is thirty centimeters squared and at B is fifteen centimeters squared — B is exactly half the area of A — so v B divided by v A equals thirty over fifteen, which equals two. <<WRITE_STEP:Continuity: v_B / v_A = 30 cm² / 15 cm² = 2  →  v_B = 2 v_A|id=ex-step-1-1>> In other words, the velocity at B is twice the velocity at A. That's our first key result. Now we apply Bernoulli's equation. Because the tube is horizontal, the gravitational potential terms cancel, and we're left with: P A plus one half rho v A squared equals P B plus one half rho v B squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Bernoulli (horizontal): P_A + ½ρv_A² = P_B + ½ρv_B²|id=ex-step-1-2>> Rearranging, P A minus P B equals one half rho v B squared minus one half rho v A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A − P_B = ½ρ(v_B² − v_A²)|id=ex-step-1-3>> We substitute v B equals two v A, so v B squared is four v A squared, and the right-hand side becomes one half rho times four v A squared minus one half rho v A squared, which simplifies to three halves rho v A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:= ½ρ(2v_A)² − ½ρv_A² = (3/2)ρv_A²|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now we plug in the numbers. The pressure difference is six hundred newtons per meter squared, and the density of water is one thousand kilograms per meter cubed. So six hundred equals three halves times one thousand times v A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:600 N/m² = (3/2) × 1000 kg/m³ × v_A²|id=ex-step-1-5>> Solving for v A squared gives us zero point four meters squared per second squared, so v A equals the square root of zero point four, which is approximately zero point six three meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:v_A² = 600 / 1500 = 0.4 m²/s²  →  v_A = √0.4 ≈ 0.63 m/s|id=ex-step-1-6>> Finally, the rate of flow is simply the area at A multiplied by the velocity at A. That's thirty centimeters squared times zero point six three meters per second. Converting consistently, this gives us one thousand eight hundred ninety cubic centimeters per second. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Rate of flow = 30 cm² × 0.63 m/s ≈ 1890 cm³/s|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> So by combining the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation, the measured pressure difference of six hundred newtons per meter squared was enough to tell us the full flow rate: one thousand eight hundred ninety cubic centimeters per second. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A tank has a cross-sectional area of zero point five meters squared and a small opening near the bottom with area one centimeter squared. A load of twenty kilograms sits on the water surface. The water level is fifty centimeters above the opening. Find the exit velocity of the water. Take g as ten meters per second squared.|id=ex-q-1>> A large tank has a cross-sectional area of zero point five meters squared, and a small opening near the bottom with a cross-sectional area of just one centimeter squared. A twenty kilogram load rests on the water surface, and the water height above the opening is fifty centimeters — that's zero point five meters. We're asked to find the speed of water coming out of the opening. Because the tank's cross-sectional area is so much larger than the opening, the speed of water inside the tank is negligible — we treat it as zero. Now, the pressure at the water surface isn't just atmospheric. The twenty kilogram load adds extra pressure. We calculate that as: force divided by area, which is twenty kilograms times ten meters per second squared, all divided by zero point five meters squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A = P₀ + (20 kg × 10 m/s²) / (0.5 m²)|id=ex-step-1-1>> That gives us an extra four hundred newtons per meter squared on top of atmospheric pressure. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A = P₀ + 400 N/m²|id=ex-step-1-2>> At the opening at the bottom, the pressure is simply atmospheric — P zero. Now we apply Bernoulli's equation between the water surface — point A — and the opening — point B. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A + ρgh + ½ρv_A² = P_B + ½ρv_B²|id=ex-step-1-3>> We substitute in: P A is P zero plus four hundred newtons per meter squared, the density of water is one thousand kilograms per meter cubed, g is ten meters per second squared, h is zero point five meters, and the speed at the surface v A is approximately zero. At the opening, P B is just P zero. <<WRITE_STEP:(P₀ + 400) + (1000)(10)(0.5) + 0 = P₀ + ½ × 1000 × v_B²|id=ex-step-1-4>> The P zero terms cancel from both sides, leaving us with four hundred plus five thousand — that's a total effective pressure of five thousand four hundred newtons per meter squared — equal to five hundred kilograms per meter cubed times v B squared. <<WRITE_STEP:5400 N/m² = 500 kg/m³ × v_B²|id=ex-step-1-5>> Solving for v B, we divide five thousand four hundred by five hundred to get v B squared equals ten point eight meters squared per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:v_B² = 5400 / 500 = 10.8 m²/s²|id=ex-step-1-6>> Taking the square root gives us the exit velocity. <<PAUSE:short>> And the answer is: the water exits at approximately three point three meters per second. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v_B ≈ 3.3 meters per second|id=ex-ans-1>> Notice how the twenty kilogram load contributed four hundred newtons per meter squared of extra pressure, which — on top of the gravitational term of five thousand newtons per meter squared from the water column — drove the total effective pressure up to five thousand four hundred newtons per meter squared, giving a faster exit speed than if there were no load at all. <<WRITE_KEY:Bernoulli → hydrostatics when v = 0 everywhere|id=key-2>>So Bernoulli's equation isn't separate from hydrostatics — hydrostatics is just Bernoulli's equation in disguise, for the special case when everything is still. One equation, two worlds. <<PAUSE:short>> So the two big ideas to lock in: first, when fluid flows, potential energy converts to kinetic energy, giving us the efflux speed of root two g h — identical to free fall. Second, when nothing flows, that same equation quietly becomes the pressure-depth rule of hydrostatics. Bernoulli is the master equation that contains both.

topics.orig_book_content:
13.1 FLUIDS
Matter is broadly divided into three categories,
solid, liquid and gas. The intermolecular forces are
strong in solids, so that the shape and size of solids
do not easily change. This force is comparatively less
in liquids and so the shape is easily changed. Although
the shape of a liquid can be easily changed, the volume
of a given mass of a liquid is not so easy to change.
It needs quite a good effort to change the density of
liquids. In gases, the intermolecular forces are very
small and it is simple to change both the shape and
the density of a gas. Liquids and gases together are
called fluids, i.e., that which can flow.
In this chapter we shall largely deal with liquids.
The equations derived may be applicable to gases in
many cases with some modifications. We shall assume
that the liquids we deal with are incompressible and
nonviscous. The first condition means that the density
of the liquid is independent of the variations in
pressure and always remains constant. The second
condition means that parts of the liquid in contact do
not exert any tangential force on each other. The force
by one part of the liquid on the other part is
perpendicular to the surface of contact. Thus, there is
no friction between the adjacent layers of a liquid.
topics.our_understanding: Let's kick off our study of fluid mechanics by getting clear on what a fluid actually is — because it's not just water in a glass. Think about the three states of matter you already know: solids, liquids, and gases. What makes them different comes down to how strongly their molecules pull on each other, which we call intermolecular forces. In a solid, these forces are very strong, which is why a brick keeps its shape and size no matter what container you put it in. In a liquid, those forces are weaker, so the shape changes easily — pour water into a bottle and it takes the bottle's shape. But here's something interesting: even though a liquid's shape changes easily, its volume is surprisingly stubborn. Try squeezing water in a sealed syringe and you'll find it barely budges. It takes a huge amount of effort to compress a liquid and change its density. Gases are the most free-spirited of the three — their intermolecular forces are very small, so you can change both the shape and the density of a gas quite easily. Think of how a balloon expands when you blow air into it. Now, liquids and gases together get a special name: fluids. The word fluid comes from the idea of flowing — anything that can flow is a fluid. So both water and air are fluids, even though they feel very different. In this chapter, we're going to focus mostly on liquids. To keep things manageable and build clean, useful equations, we'll make two important simplifying assumptions. First, we'll treat our liquids as incompressible, meaning the density stays constant no matter how the pressure changes. Second, we'll treat them as nonviscous, meaning there's no friction between neighboring layers of the liquid. When one layer of liquid slides past another, they don't drag on each other at all. The force between any two parts of a liquid acts perpendicular to the surface between them — never along it. These two assumptions let us develop powerful ideas that apply surprisingly well to real liquids like water, and even to gases in many situations with a few tweaks. Keep these two ideas — incompressible and nonviscous — in the back of your mind as we move forward, because they'll show up again and again.

events.text: Solid — strong intermolecular forces → fixed shape AND fixed volume
Liquid — weaker forces → shape changes freely, volume stays fixed
Fluids = liquids + gases (both flow; liquids are nearly incompressible)
Ideal fluid: force between layers is always perpendicular — no sideways friction
Incompressible + non-viscous: the two assumptions we carry forward

That tension between 'flows easily' and 'resists squeezing' is exactly what makes liquids so fascinating — and so useful in engineering.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about pressure in a fluid — what it actually means, how we define it precisely, and how it changes as you move up or down through a liquid or gas. Imagine you pick any point inside a fluid, say a point deep inside a tank of water. Around that point, picture a tiny little patch of area. The fluid on one side of that patch pushes on the fluid on the other side, and the other side pushes back. Pressure at that point is defined as the force divided by that tiny area, as the area shrinks down to essentially nothing. That limiting process gives us a clean, precise value at exactly one point. Now here is something really important: for a smooth, uniform fluid that has no internal friction — what we call a homogeneous and nonviscous fluid — this pressure value does not depend on which direction you tilt that tiny patch. It comes out the same no matter the orientation. That is why pressure is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude only, no direction attached to it. The SI unit of pressure is newtons per meter squared, which we call the pascal, abbreviated Pa. Now, how does pressure change as you move up or down in a fluid? Think about a thin horizontal slab of fluid sitting somewhere inside a tank. The fluid below it pushes up, the fluid above it pushes down, and the weight of the slab itself pulls it downward. For the slab to stay still — to be in equilibrium — those forces must balance. When you work through that balance carefully, you find that as you move upward by a tiny height, the pressure drops by an amount equal to the fluid's density times gravitational acceleration times that tiny height. In other words, going up means lower pressure, going down means higher pressure. If the density of the fluid stays the same throughout — which is a good assumption for liquids — then the pressure difference between two heights is simply density times g times the vertical distance between them. This is one of the most useful results in all of fluid mechanics. Finally, think about two points sitting at exactly the same height inside a connected fluid. If you imagine a horizontal cylinder of fluid connecting those two points, the only horizontal forces are the pressure forces from each end. For the fluid to stay put, those forces must be equal, which means the pressures must be equal. So here is the rule to remember: pressure increases as you go deeper, and pressure is the same at any two points that are at the same height in a connected fluid. These two ideas together let you solve a huge range of real-world problems involving liquids and gases.

That single observation is going to unlock everything about pressure in a fluid. <<FOCUS:point-a>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_2:pressure_point>> <<SECTION:Pressure at a Point|id=sec-1>>Let's pick any point inside a body of fluid — call it point A. Now imagine a tiny flat patch of area sitting around that point. The fluid on one side of the patch shoves the fluid on the other side, and the other side shoves back. The force per unit area — as we shrink that patch down to nothing — is what we call the pressure at point A. <<WRITE_TEXT:Pressure = Force ÷ Area (as area → 0)|id=text-1>>So pressure is defined as P equals the limit of F divided by delta S, as delta S shrinks to zero. It's the force squeezing through an infinitely small window of area. <<POINT:area-horizontal>> Pressure at a point is the force pushing through a tiny area patch, divided by that area, as the patch shrinks to essentially nothing. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P = \lim_{\Delta S \to 0} \frac{F}{\Delta S}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:area-tilted>> Now here's the really surprising part. What if we tilt that tiny patch? Rotate it forty-five degrees, or ninety degrees, or any angle at all — the pressure value doesn't change. For a smooth fluid with no internal friction, the pressure at a point is completely independent of which direction you face your little area patch. <<TRACE:area-tilted>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Pressure has NO direction — same in all orientations|id=key-1>>That's what it means to say pressure is a scalar. Not a vector. No arrow. No direction. Just a number — the same number no matter which way you slice through the fluid at that point. That's exactly why your ears feel equally squeezed from every direction when you're deep underwater. <<POINT:equal-pressure-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:fluid-column>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_2:pressure_depth>> <<SECTION:Pressure vs Depth|id=sec-2>>Now for the next question: does pressure change as you move up or down in a fluid? <<PAUSE:long>> Picture a short slab of fluid trapped between two horizontal layers — layer A at the bottom and layer B at the top, separated by a tiny height dz. Three forces act on this slab vertically. The fluid below pushes it up with force F one. The fluid above pushes it down with force F two. And gravity pulls the slab's own weight straight down. <<TRACE:fluid-column>> <<POINT:fluid-column>> <<FOCUS:f1-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:F1 (up) = P·ΔS|id=step-1>>F one pushing up equals the pressure P at level A times the area delta S. And F two pushing down equals the pressure at level B — call it P plus dP — times the same area. <<FOCUS:f2-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:F2 (down) = (P+dP)·ΔS|id=step-2>>The slab isn't accelerating — it's just sitting there in equilibrium. So the net upward force must be zero. That means F one minus F two minus W equals zero. <<FOCUS:weight-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:dP/dz = −ρg|id=step-3>>The weight W of the slab is density rho times g times the volume, which is delta S times dz. When you substitute everything in and simplify, you get: dP equals negative rho times g times dz. The negative sign tells you pressure drops as you go UP — or equivalently, pressure rises as you go DOWN. <<POINT:weight-arrow>> The pressure change over a tiny vertical distance equals negative the fluid density times gravitational acceleration — so pressure falls as you rise, and grows as you descend. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{dP}{dz} = -\rho g|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Deeper → more weight above → higher pressure|id=key-2>>Think about it physically: every extra meter of water above you adds more weight pressing down. That's all the equation is saying. Dive twice as deep, and there's twice as much water sitting on top of you, so the pressure is roughly twice as large. <<TRACE:depth-gradient-label>> <<POINT:depth-gradient-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter that builds the core result for pressure variation with depth. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Derive how pressure varies with height in a static fluid, and find the pressure difference between two levels separated by height h.|id=ex-q-1>> We consider two horizontal surfaces — call them delta S one and delta S two — separated by a small vertical height d z. Point A sits on the lower surface, and point B sits on the upper surface. The pressure at lower surface A is P, and the pressure at upper surface B is P plus d P. Now let's identify the three vertical forces acting on the fluid enclosed between those two surfaces. <<WRITE_STEP:Forces on enclosed fluid:|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:F1 (upward, from fluid below)  = P × ΔS|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:F2 (downward, from fluid above) = (P + dP) × ΔS|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:W  (downward weight)           = ρ × ΔS × dz × g|id=ex-step-1-4>> The upward force F one equals P times delta S, the downward force F two equals open bracket P plus d P close bracket times delta S, and the weight W of the enclosed fluid equals rho times delta S times d z times g, since the volume of that little slab is delta S times d z. For the fluid to be in vertical equilibrium, the upward force must balance the two downward forces. So we write F one equals F two plus W. <<WRITE_STEP:Vertical equilibrium: F1 = F2 + W|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<WRITE_STEP:⟹  P × ΔS = (P + dP) × ΔS + ρg dz ΔS|id=ex-step-1-6>> Expanding the right-hand side, P times delta S equals P times delta S plus d P times delta S plus rho times g times d z times delta S. The P times delta S terms cancel on both sides, and dividing through by delta S we get d P equals negative rho times g times d z. <<WRITE_STEP:⟹  dP = −ρ g dz|id=ex-step-1-7>> This tells us that as we move upward through a height d z, the pressure decreases by rho times g times d z — pressure decreases as height increases. Now we integrate this result between two levels. Take z equals zero at the bottom with pressure P one, and z equals h at the top with pressure P two. <<WRITE_STEP:Integrate from z = 0 (pressure P1) to z = h (pressure P2):|id=ex-step-1-8>> <<WRITE_STEP:∫dP = −∫ρg dz  ⟹  P2 − P1 = −ρgh   (uniform density)|id=ex-step-1-9>> For a fluid of uniform density rho, the integral on the right is just rho times g times h, giving P two minus P one equals negative rho times g times h, or equivalently P one minus P two equals rho times g times h. And there is our key result. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:P1 − P2 = ρ g h  (pressure difference between two levels of height h in a uniform-density fluid)|id=ex-ans-1>> The pressure difference between any two horizontal levels in a uniform-density fluid equals rho times g times h, where h is the vertical height separating them. The deeper level always has the higher pressure, which is exactly what we expect: every extra layer of fluid above you adds weight, and that weight drives the pressure up. Here's an example straight from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Two points A and B lie at the same horizontal level inside a fluid in equilibrium. Show that the pressure at A equals the pressure at B.|id=ex-q-1>> Consider two points A and B at the same horizontal level inside a fluid. We imagine a small vertical area S containing point A, and an equal small vertical area S containing point B — so both cross-sectional areas are the same value, which we call S. Now picture the horizontal cylinder of fluid that connects the two points — it's bounded on the left by area S at point A and on the right by area S at point B. The fluid to the left pushes on this cylinder with a force equal to P one times S, directed towards the right. The fluid to the right pushes back with a force equal to P two times S, directed towards the left. <<WRITE_STEP:Force on left end  = P₁ × S  (directed right)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Force on right end = P₂ × S  (directed left)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Because the fluid is in equilibrium, these two forces must balance each other exactly. So the equilibrium condition gives us P one times S equals P two times S. <<WRITE_STEP:Equilibrium condition:  P₁S = P₂S|id=ex-step-1-3>> We can divide both sides by S, and S cancels out completely, leaving us with P one equals P two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:P₁ = P₂  →  Pressure is the same at any two points on the same horizontal level.|id=ex-ans-1>> And that is the conclusion: any two points at the same horizontal level inside a fluid in equilibrium have exactly the same pressure. <<PAUSE:short>> So here's the payoff to our opening mystery: your ears pop going deeper because there's more fluid above you — more weight, more pressure — and that pressure squeezes from every direction at once, because pressure at a point is a scalar with no preferred direction. <<POINT:dz-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:SI unit: pascal (Pa) = N per m²|id=text-2>>One last thing to lock in: pressure is measured in pascals. One pascal equals one newton per square meter. It's named after Blaise Pascal — who, not coincidentally, is exactly the person we'll talk about in the next topic.
