topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the most elegant ideas in fluid mechanics — Pascal's Law. Here's the key insight: when you have a liquid sitting still in a container, the pressure difference between any two points depends only on how far apart they are vertically. Now, imagine you push down on that liquid somewhere — you increase the pressure at that spot. What happens everywhere else? The pressure goes up by exactly the same amount. That's Pascal's Law in a nutshell: any change in pressure at one point in a liquid is transmitted equally to every single point in that liquid, without losing any strength along the way.

Think about why this makes sense. The pressure at a deeper point is always a fixed amount more than the pressure at a shallower point — that fixed amount depends on the density of the liquid and the vertical distance between them. If you push down and raise the pressure at the top, the pressure at the bottom has to rise by the same amount to keep that difference intact. The liquid is incompressible, so the vertical distances don't change, and the pressure difference stays the same. The only way that works is if both pressures go up equally.

Now here's where it gets really exciting — the hydraulic lift. We'll look at the diagram in a moment, but picture two cylinders of different sizes connected by a tube filled with liquid. One cylinder is narrow, one is wide. You push down on the narrow piston with a small force. That creates a pressure increase throughout the liquid. On the wide side, that same pressure increase acts over a much bigger area, so it produces a much bigger force — big enough to lift a car! The force on the wide piston equals the pressure increase multiplied by the larger area.

Here's the honest part though — you don't get something for nothing. The work done on both sides is the same. To get a bigger force on the wide side, you have to push the narrow piston down a much greater distance. Force times distance stays constant. Pascal's Law gives you a mechanical advantage in force, but the energy in equals the energy out. This principle is used in car lifts, hydraulic brakes, and heavy machinery all around you.

If the cross-sectional area of the piston is A, the pressure just below the piston is increased by F/A. By Pascal's law, the pressure at any point B will also increase by the same amount F/A. This is because the pressure at B has to be gz more than the pressure at the piston, where z is the vertical distance of B below the piston. By applying the force we do not appreciably change z (as the liquid is supposed to be incompressible) and hence the pressure difference remains unchanged. As the pressure at the piston is increased by F/A, the pressure at B also increases by the same amount.

This is Pascal's Law in action: an external pressure change applied anywhere in an enclosed, incompressible liquid is transmitted equally to every point in that liquid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Pressure increase at B = F / A   (same as at the piston, because z is unchanged)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter on Pascal's Law — the hydraulic lift. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A hydraulic lift has two vertical cylinders A and B with cross-sectional areas A1 and A2. A force F1 is applied to the narrow piston A. What force F2 is produced on the wider piston B, and is any energy gained?|id=ex-q-1>> We have two cylinders, A and B, connected by a horizontal tube. Cylinder A has cross-sectional area A1, and cylinder B has cross-sectional area A2, where A2 is larger than A1. The load sits on the piston of the larger area A2. A liquid fills the system. We start by finding the pressure increase caused by pushing on piston A. When a force F1 is applied to piston A, by Pascal's Law, the pressure increases everywhere in the liquid by the same amount — that increase is F1 divided by A1. <<WRITE_STEP:Pressure increase = F1 / A1   (transmitted equally throughout the liquid)|id=ex-step-1-1>> This uniform pressure rise is the key: every part of the fluid, including the face of the wider piston B, feels that same extra pressure. Now we find the force this pressure produces on the larger piston B. Force equals pressure times area, so the extra force F2 acting upward on piston B is A2 times the quantity F1 divided by A1. <<WRITE_STEP:F2 = A2 × (F1 / A1)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Because A2 is larger than A1, F2 is larger than F1. In fact, if A2 is much larger than A1, then F2 is much larger than F1 — even a small applied force can raise a heavy load. This is the mechanical advantage of the hydraulic lift. But we must check: is any energy being created here? The answer is no. The work done by F1 equals the work done by F2 — there is no gain in energy. <<WRITE_STEP:Work done by F1 = Work done by F2   (no energy gain)|id=ex-step-1-3>> How does this balance out? Piston A must move downward a larger distance compared to the height that piston B moves up. So you trade a smaller force over a longer distance for a larger force over a shorter distance — exactly like any other simple machine. So to summarise the result: <<WRITE_ANSWER:F2 = A2 × (F1 / A1). Since A2 > A1, the hydraulic lift multiplies force — but work in equals work out, and piston A travels a greater distance than piston B.|id=ex-ans-1>> The force on the large piston F2 equals A2 times F1 divided by A1. The larger the ratio of A2 to A1, the greater the force multiplication. And the energy books always balance — piston A moves down a larger distance than piston B moves up, keeping the total work equal on both sides. <<FOCUS:output-force-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Force multiplication: F_out = f × (A/a)|id=key-2>>This is the power of Pascal's Law in action. The same pressure — transmitted equally everywhere — acts on a huge area and produces a huge force. That's how a small finger lifts a tonne of car. <<POINT:output-force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the elegant core idea is this: a still liquid cannot absorb or hide a pressure change — it must pass it on, perfectly and equally, to every corner of the container. That one fact is Pascal's Law, and it's the reason hydraulic brakes, car lifts, and dentist chairs all work.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something you experience every single moment of your life without even noticing — the weight of the air above you pressing down on your body. That's atmospheric pressure. The atmosphere stretches up to about two hundred kilometers above the earth's surface, and all that air has weight. That weight pushes down on every surface it touches, and the force is always perpendicular to whatever surface the air is in contact with. At the very top of the atmosphere, the pressure is zero because there's nothing above it pushing down. As you go deeper into the atmosphere — closer to the ground — more and more air is stacked above you, so the pressure increases. Now, because air is not very dense, the pressure doesn't change much over small distances near the ground. That's why we can say the atmospheric pressure in a city is about seventy-six centimeters of mercury without worrying about whether you're standing at ground level or on top of a building — the difference is tiny.

Now, how do we actually measure this pressure? A scientist named Torricelli came up with a beautifully clever device called a barometer. Here's how it works. You take a glass tube about a meter long, fill it completely with mercury, seal the open end temporarily, and then flip it upside down into a cup of mercury. When you remove the seal, something interesting happens — the mercury column inside the tube drops a little and then stops. The space left at the top of the tube is a vacuum, meaning there's no air and no pressure there at all. We'll look at the diagram in a moment to see this clearly.

Now think about two points at the same horizontal level — one inside the tube and one on the open surface of mercury in the cup. The point in the cup is exposed to the atmosphere, so the pressure there equals atmospheric pressure. Since both points are at the same height, the pressure must be equal at both. So the pressure at the point inside the tube, at the level of the cup's surface, also equals atmospheric pressure. But we know the pressure at the very top of the mercury column inside the tube is zero — it's a vacuum. So all the pressure at the bottom of that column must come from the weight of the mercury above it. Using the pressure-depth relationship, atmospheric pressure equals the density of mercury times g times the height of the mercury column. That height turns out to be about seventy-six centimeters under normal conditions. Plugging in the density of mercury as thirteen thousand six hundred kilograms per cubic meter, g as nine point eight meters per second squared, and the height as zero point seven six meters, you get about one point zero one times ten to the power five pascals. This is defined as one atmosphere of pressure. A related device called a manometer works on the same principle to measure the pressure of a gas trapped in a closed container, by comparing it to atmospheric pressure using the difference in liquid levels in a U-shaped tube.

Water is filled in a flask up to a height of 20 cm. The bottom of the flask is circular with radius 10 cm. If the atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10^5 Pa, find the force exerted by the water on the bottom. Take g = 10 m s^−2 and density of water = 1000 kg m^−3.

P = P0 + hρg
= 1.01 × 10^5 Pa + 0.20 m × 1000 kg m^−3 × 10 m s^−2
= 1.01 × 10^5 Pa + 0.02 × 10^5 Pa
= 1.03 × 10^5 Pa.
The area of the bottom = πr^2 = 3.14 × (0.1 m)^2 = 0.0314 m^2.
The force on the bottom is, therefore,
F = P × πr^2
= 1.03 × 10^5 Pa × 0.0314 m^2 = 3230 N.

13.5 ARCHIMEDES’ PRINCIPLE
When a body is partially or fully dipped into a
fluid, the fluid exerts forces on the body. At any small
portion of the surface of the body, the force by the fluid
is perpendicular to the surface and is equal to the
pressure at that point multiplied by the area (figure
13.8). The resultant of all these contact forces is called
the force of buoyancy or buoyant force.
Archimedes’ principle states that when a body is
partially or fully dipped into a fluid at rest, the fluid
exerts an upward force of buoyancy equal to the weight
of the displaced fluid.
Archimedes’ principle is not an independent
principle and may be deduced from Newton’s laws of
motion.
Consider the situation shown in figure (13.8) where
a body is shown dipped into a fluid. Suppose the body
dipped in the fluid is replaced by the same fluid of
equal volume. As the entire fluid now becomes
homogeneous, all parts will remain in equilibrium. The
part of the fluid substituting the body also remains in
equilibrium. Forces acting on this substituting fluid
are
(a) the weight mg of this part of the fluid, and
(b) the resultant B of the contact forces by the
remaining fluid.
As the substituting fluid is in equilibrium, these
two should be equal and opposite. Thus,
              B  mg
 (13.5)
and it acts in the vertically upward direction. 
Now the substituting fluid just occupies the space
which was previously occupied by the body. Hence, the
shape of the boundary of the substituting fluid is same
as the boundary of the body. Thus, the magnitude and
direction of the force due to the pressure on any small
area of the boundary is same for the body as for the
substituting fluid. The force of buoyancy on the body
is, therefore, same as the force of buoyancy B on the
substituting fluid.
From equation (13.5) the force of buoyancy on a
dipped body is equal to the weight mg of the displaced
fluid and acts along the vertically upward direction.
This is Archimedes’ principle.
Note that in this derivation we have assumed that
the fluid is in equilibrium in an inertial frame. If it is
not so, the force of buoyancy may be different from the
weight of the displaced fluid.
Floatation
When a solid body is dipped into a fluid, the fluid
exerts an upward force of buoyancy on the solid. If the
force of buoyancy equals the weight of the solid, the
solid will remain in equilibrium. This is called
floatation. When the overall density of the solid is
smaller than the density of the fluid, the solid floats
with a part of it in the fluid. The fraction dipped is
such that the weight of the displaced fluid equals the
weight of the solid.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the most famous ideas in all of physics — Archimedes' principle. Imagine you drop a rock into a bucket of water. You can feel that the rock seems lighter when it's underwater, right? That's buoyancy at work. When any object is partially or fully submerged in a fluid, the fluid pushes back on it from all sides. Every tiny patch of the object's surface feels a force from the fluid, and that force is always perpendicular to the surface. When you add up all those tiny pushes, the net result is a single upward force — we call this the buoyant force.

Archimedes' principle tells us exactly how big that buoyant force is. It says the upward buoyant force on a submerged object equals the weight of the fluid that the object displaces. In other words, if you push an object into water and it shoves aside, say, half a litre of water, the buoyant force equals the weight of that half litre of water. Simple and powerful.

Now here's the beautiful part — this principle isn't just something we accept on faith. We can actually derive it from Newton's laws. Think about it this way: imagine you replace the submerged object with an equal volume of the same fluid. Now the whole container is just fluid, and everything is in equilibrium. That blob of fluid sitting in the same spot must be perfectly balanced — its weight pulls it down, and the surrounding fluid pushes it up with a force B. Since it's in equilibrium, B must exactly equal the weight of that blob of fluid. And here's the key insight: the forces on the boundary of that blob are identical whether the blob is made of fluid or of your original solid object, because the shape of the boundary is the same. So the buoyant force on your original object must also equal the weight of the displaced fluid. That's the whole derivation.

One important note — this derivation assumes the fluid itself is sitting still in a non-accelerating environment. If the fluid is accelerating, things get more complicated.

Now let's talk about floating. When you place a solid in a fluid, if the buoyant force exactly equals the object's weight, the object floats in equilibrium. If the object's overall density is less than the fluid's density, it will float with only part of it submerged. The fraction that dips below the surface adjusts itself until the weight of the displaced fluid exactly matches the weight of the solid. That's why a massive ship made of steel can float — its overall density, counting all the hollow air-filled space inside, is less than the density of water. We'll look at a worked example in a moment that makes this beautifully concrete.

book_examples.verbatim_text:
Example 13.2
A 700 g solid cube having an edge of length 10 cm floats in water. How much volume of the cube is outside the water? Density of water = 1000 kg m^-3.
Solution: The weight of the cube is balanced by the buoyant force. The buoyant force is equal to the weight of the water displaced. If a volume V of the cube is inside the water, the weight of the displaced water = V * rho * g, where rho is the density of water. Thus,
V * rho * g = 0.7 kg * g
or, V = 0.7 kg / rho = 0.7 kg / 1000 kg m^-3 = 7 x 10^-4 m^3 = 700 cm^3.
The total volume of the cube = (10 cm)^3 = 1000 cm^3.
The volume outside the water is
1000 cm^3 - 700 cm^3 = 300 cm^3.

events.title: Buoyancy — the upward push of a fluid

events.text: Fluid presses on every face of a submerged object
Deeper → higher pressure → stronger upward push
How big is the buoyant force?
Replace body with same-shaped fluid → equilibrium
Buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid
Same boundary → same contact forces → same B
Archimedes' principle follows from Newton's laws
B depends on: fluid density × submerged volume × g
Q: A 700 gram solid cube with edge length 10 centimeters floats in water. How much of the cube's volume is outside the water? Density of water equals 1000 kilograms per cubic meter.
Buoyant force = weight of displaced water = V × ρ × g

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:fluid-container>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_5:buoyancy_diagram>> Have you ever noticed that lifting a heavy rock underwater feels almost effortless — but the moment you lift it out, it suddenly feels crushing? The water is doing something remarkable. What exactly is it pushing against? <<SECTION:Buoyancy — the upward push of a fluid|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:submerged-body>> Here is our setup. A solid block sitting fully underwater inside a tank of fluid. The fluid is in contact with every face of that block — top, bottom, left, right. <<WRITE_TEXT:Fluid presses on every face of a submerged object|id=text-1>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrows-sides>> The side forces — left and right — push equally hard toward the center. They cancel each other out perfectly. Nothing net happening horizontally. <<POINT:pressure-arrows-sides>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrow-top>> But look at the top and bottom faces. The bottom of the block sits deeper in the fluid. Deeper means higher pressure. So the upward push on the bottom is stronger than the downward push on the top. <<WRITE_TEXT:Deeper → higher pressure → stronger upward push|id=text-2>> <<POINT:pressure-arrow-top>> <<FOCUS:buoyant-force-arrow>> When you add up every tiny force the fluid exerts on the block, all the sideways contributions cancel — and what survives is one single net force pointing straight up. That surviving force is what we call the buoyant force. <<TRACE:buoyant-force-arrow>> Now here is the brilliant question Archimedes answered: how BIG is that upward force? <<WRITE_TEXT:How big is the buoyant force?|id=text-3>> <<POINT:buoyant-force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:displaced-fluid-region>> Imagine scooping the solid block out and pouring fluid back in to fill the exact same shape — the same volume, the same boundary. Now the whole tank is just fluid again. That filled-in region sits perfectly still. It is in equilibrium. <<WRITE_TEXT:Replace body with same-shaped fluid → equilibrium|id=text-4>> <<TRACE:displaced-fluid-region>> The buoyant force B equals the weight of the fluid that was shoved aside — the displaced fluid's mass times g. <<WRITE_EQUATION:B = mg_{\text{displaced fluid}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:weight-displaced-label>> Two forces act on that imaginary plug of fluid: its own weight pulling it down, and the push from all the surrounding fluid. Because it is not moving, those two forces must be exactly equal and opposite. The buoyant force B equals the weight of that plug — the weight of the displaced fluid. <<WRITE_KEY:Buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid|id=key-1>> <<POINT:weight-displaced-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:submerged-body>> And here is the elegant part — the surrounding fluid does not care whether that space is filled with our imaginary plug of fluid OR with the original solid block. The boundary is identical, so the contact forces are identical. The buoyant force on the real block is exactly the same. <<WRITE_TEXT:Same boundary → same contact forces → same B|id=text-5>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> This means Archimedes' principle is not a mysterious new law — it falls straight out of Newton's laws. If the substituted fluid is in balance, the forces on the real object must be the same. <<WRITE_KEY:Archimedes' principle follows from Newton's laws|id=key-2>> <<SECTION:What controls the buoyant force|id=sec-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:displaced-fluid-region>> So what actually controls how large the buoyant force is? Only two things: the density of the fluid, and the volume of the object that is submerged. The material of the object — steel, wood, rubber — is irrelevant. Only the displaced volume matters. <<WRITE_TEXT:B depends on: fluid density × submerged volume × g|id=text-6>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A 700 gram solid cube with edge length 10 centimeters floats in water. How much of the cube's volume is outside the water? Density of water equals 1000 kilograms per cubic meter.|id=ex-q-1>> A solid cube has a mass of seven hundred grams, that's zero point seven kilograms, and each edge is ten centimeters long. It's floating in water, and we want to find how much of that cube sits above the surface. We start by recognising that the cube is in equilibrium — so the buoyant force exactly equals the weight of the cube. And by Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force equals the weight of the water displaced. If a volume V of the cube is submerged, the weight of the displaced water equals V times rho times g, where rho is the density of water. <<WRITE_STEP:Buoyant force = weight of displaced water = V × ρ × g|id=ex-step-1-1>> Setting that equal to the weight of the cube gives us V times rho times g equals zero point seven kilograms times g. <<WRITE_STEP:V × ρ × g = 0.7 kg × g|id=ex-step-1-2>> Notice that g cancels from both sides, which is very convenient. So we get V equals zero point seven kilograms divided by rho, which is zero point seven kilograms divided by one thousand kilograms per cubic meter. <<WRITE_STEP:V = 0.7 kg ÷ 1000 kg/m³ = 7 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = 700 cm³|id=ex-step-1-3>> That works out to seven times ten to the power of negative four cubic meters, which is the same as seven hundred cubic centimeters. So seven hundred cubic centimeters of the cube is submerged underwater. Now let's find the total volume of the cube. The edge length is ten centimeters, so the total volume is ten cubed, which equals one thousand cubic centimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:Total volume = 10³ = 1000 cm³|id=ex-step-1-4>> The volume outside the water is simply the total volume minus the submerged volume — that's one thousand minus seven hundred, which equals three hundred cubic centimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:Volume outside water = 1000 − 700 = 300 cm³|id=ex-step-1-5>> And there's our answer. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Volume outside water = 300 cubic centimeters|id=ex-ans-1>> Three hundred cubic centimeters of the cube sits above the water surface. That's thirty percent of the cube peeking out — which makes sense, since the cube's effective density is seven hundred kilograms per cubic meter, less than water's one thousand kilograms per cubic meter, so it floats with just the right fraction submerged to balance its weight. That is why a massive steel ship floats. Its hull is shaped to displace a huge volume of water — enough that the weight of all that displaced water exceeds the ship's own weight. The ocean pushes back harder than gravity pulls down. <<POINT:buoyant-force-arrow>> <<FOCUS:buoyant-force-arrow>> So the one thing to lock in: the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid — nothing more, nothing less. Bigger displaced volume, bigger buoyant force. Denser fluid, bigger buoyant force. That single idea explains floating, sinking, and everything in between. <<WRITE_KEY:B = weight of displaced fluid — the one rule for floating and sinking|id=key-3>> <<PAUSE:short>>

Equations (13.3) and (13.5) were derived by
assuming that the fluid under consideration is in
equilibrium in an inertial frame. If this is not the case,
the equations must be modified. We shall discuss some
special cases of accelerating fluids.
A Liquid Placed in an Elevator
(a) Pressure Difference
Suppose a beaker contains some liquid and it is
placed in an elevator which is going up with an
acceleration a0 (figure 13.9). Let A and B be two points
in the liquid, B being at a vertical height z above A.
Construct a small horizontal area S around A and an
equal horizontal area around B. Construct a vertical
cylinder with the two areas as the faces. Consider the
motion of the liquid contained within this cylinder. Let
P1 be the pressure at A and P2 be the pressure at B.
Forces acting on the liquid contained in the
cylinder, in the vertical direction, are :
(a) P1S, upward due to the liquid below it
(b) P2S, downward due to the liquid above it and
(c) weight mg  Szg downward, where  is the
density of the liquid.
Under the action of these three forces the liquid is

Newton’s second law

liquid of equal volume. The entire liquid becomes a

at rest with respect to the rest of the liquid. Thus, the
substituted liquid is also going up with an acceleration

The forces acting on the substituted liquid are
(a) the buoyant force B and
(b) the weight mg of the substituted liquid.

B  mg  a0

Equation (13.6) and (13.7) are similar to the

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens to fluids when they're not just sitting still — when they're accelerating. Up until now, we've been thinking about fluids in calm, stationary situations. But what if you put a glass of water in an elevator that's speeding upward? Or what if you slide a beaker of water across a table and it accelerates horizontally? The pressure inside that fluid changes in interesting ways, and that's exactly what this section is about.

Let's start with the elevator going upward with some acceleration. Imagine two points inside the liquid — call them A and B, where B is directly above A. If you think about a tiny column of liquid between those two points, three forces act on it vertically: the pressure from below pushing up, the pressure from above pushing down, and gravity pulling the whole column down. But now, unlike a stationary situation, this column is also accelerating upward. So when we apply Newton's second law, we find that the pressure difference between A and B equals the density of the liquid times the quantity g plus a, all multiplied by the vertical distance between them. Notice that this is just like the normal pressure formula, except that g plus a takes the place of plain g. The fluid behaves as if gravity has gotten stronger. That makes intuitive sense — when an elevator accelerates upward, you feel heavier, and so does the fluid.

The same idea applies to buoyancy. If you submerge an object in that accelerating liquid, the buoyant force turns out to be the mass of displaced fluid times g plus a, rather than just g. Again, it's as if effective gravity has increased.

Now let's think about horizontal acceleration. Imagine a beaker of water sliding forward with some horizontal acceleration. Pick two points at the same height inside the liquid, separated horizontally along the direction of motion. You might expect equal pressure at equal heights — but no! Because the liquid itself is being pushed forward, there's a net horizontal force on any little chunk of it, which means there must be a pressure difference driving it. The pressure is higher on the side that's being pushed into, and lower on the side ahead.

Here's the really striking consequence: the free surface of the liquid — the top surface — is no longer flat and horizontal. It tilts. The back of the beaker has a higher liquid level, and the front has a lower one. We can actually calculate the angle of that tilt. It turns out that the tangent of the tilt angle equals the horizontal acceleration divided by g. So a stronger acceleration means a steeper tilt. We'll look at the diagram in a moment to see this clearly. This is a beautiful result — the geometry of the liquid surface directly tells you the ratio of horizontal acceleration to gravitational acceleration.

events.title: Buoyant Force in an Accelerating Fluid

events.text: Q: A beaker of liquid is in an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Points A and B are in the liquid, with B at vertical height z above A. The liquid has density rho. Find the pressure difference P1 minus P2 between A and B.
Forces on the cylinder (vertical direction):
(a) P1 times S — upward, from liquid below
(b) P2 times S — downward, from liquid above
(c) weight = S times z times rho times g — downward
Newton's second law (upward positive):
P1·S − P2·S − S·z·rho·g = S·z·rho·a0
(P1 − P2)·S = S·z·rho·g + S·z·rho·a0
P1 − P2 = rho·(g + a0)·z
P1 − P2 = rho × (g + a0) × z
Q: A body is fully submerged in a liquid of density rho, inside an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Find the buoyant force B on the body.
Substituted liquid: mass m = mass of displaced liquid, accelerating upward at a0
Forces on substituted liquid: (a) Buoyant force B — upward, (b) Weight mg — downward
Newton's second law → B − mg = m times a0
Rearranging → B = m times g + m times a0 = m times (g + a0)
B = m(g + a0), where m is the mass of the displaced liquid

Q: A beaker of liquid accelerates horizontally with acceleration a0. Points A and B are at the same horizontal level, separated by distance l along the direction of acceleration. The liquid has density rho. Find the tilt angle theta of the free surface.
(P1 − P2)ΔS = (ΔS) · l · ρ · a0
P1 − P2 = l · ρ · a0
P1 = P0 + h1·ρ·g,   P2 = P0 + h2·ρ·g
tan θ = (h1 − h2) / l = a0 / g
tan θ = a0 / g  (theta = tilt angle of the free surface)
Buoyant force = ρV(g + a₀) in accelerating fluid
Free fall: a₀ = −g → buoyancy = 0

So according to Newton's second law, the NET upward force on it must equal m times a zero, not zero. How does that change the pressure difference? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:height-z>> <<WRITE_STEP:P1·S − P2·S − mg = m·a0|id=step-1>>Newton's second law says: P one S minus P two S minus m g equals m times a zero. Rearranging, the pressure difference P one minus P two equals rho times the quantity g plus a zero, all times z — where rho is the density of the liquid. <<PAUSE:short>> The net upward force must drive the acceleration, so the pressure difference picks up an extra a zero term alongside g — giving us an effective gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_1 - P_2 = \rho(g + a_0)z|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:fluid-cylinder>> <<WRITE_KEY:P1 − P2 = ρ(g + a₀)z — effective gravity replaces g|id=key-1>>Notice what happened: gravity g just got replaced by an 'effective gravity' of g plus a zero. The fluid acts as though gravity itself got stronger. That's why your water feels heavier in an upward-accelerating elevator. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:elevator-box>> <<SECTION:Buoyant Force in an Accelerating Fluid|id=sec-2>>Now let's think about buoyancy. You already know from Archimedes' principle that the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid — rho times V times g. But that was for a stationary fluid. <<FOCUS:fluid-cylinder>> In the accelerating elevator, every pressure force on a submerged object scales with that same effective gravity g plus a zero. So the net upward pressure force — the buoyant force — becomes rho times V times the quantity g plus a zero. <<PAUSE:short>> Since every pressure in the fluid now scales with effective gravity, the buoyant force formula simply replaces g with g plus a zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{buoyant}} = \rho V (g + a_0)|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A beaker of liquid is in an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Points A and B are in the liquid, with B at vertical height z above A. The liquid has density rho. Find the pressure difference P1 minus P2 between A and B.|id=ex-q-1>> Suppose a beaker contains some liquid placed in an elevator going up with an acceleration a0. We have two points, A and B, inside the liquid, where B is at a vertical height z above A. The pressure at A is P1 and the pressure at B is P2, and the liquid has density rho. We isolate a small vertical cylinder of liquid with a horizontal cross-sectional area S at each face — one face at A, one face at B. Now let's list the three vertical forces acting on this cylinder of liquid. <<WRITE_STEP:Forces on the cylinder (vertical direction):|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:(a) P1 times S — upward, from liquid below|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_STEP:(b) P2 times S — downward, from liquid above|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:(c) weight = S times z times rho times g — downward|id=ex-step-1-4>> First, P1 times S acts upward due to the liquid below the cylinder. Second, P2 times S acts downward due to the liquid above it. And third, the weight of the liquid in the cylinder acts downward — that weight equals the volume S times z, multiplied by density rho, multiplied by g. Now, the entire elevator — and therefore this cylinder of liquid — is accelerating upward with acceleration a0. So we apply Newton's second law in the vertical direction. The net upward force equals mass times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:Newton's second law (upward positive):|id=ex-step-1-5>> <<WRITE_STEP:P1·S − P2·S − S·z·rho·g = S·z·rho·a0|id=ex-step-1-6>> The left-hand side has P1 times S upward, minus P2 times S downward, minus the weight S times z times rho times g downward. The right-hand side is the mass S times z times rho, multiplied by a0. Let's rearrange. We bring the weight term to the right-hand side, so the right side becomes mass times g plus mass times a0. Then we factor out S times z times rho on the right, and divide both sides by S. <<WRITE_STEP:(P1 − P2)·S = S·z·rho·g + S·z·rho·a0|id=ex-step-1-7>> <<WRITE_STEP:P1 − P2 = rho·(g + a0)·z|id=ex-step-1-8>> <<PAUSE:short>> Dividing through by S, we get P1 minus P2 equals rho times the quantity g plus a0, times z. Notice this is exactly like the static pressure formula, except gravity g has been effectively replaced by g plus a0 — the upward acceleration adds to gravity. And so the final result is: <<WRITE_ANSWER:P1 − P2 = rho × (g + a0) × z|id=ex-ans-1>> The pressure difference between point A and point B, where B is a vertical height z above A, is rho times the quantity g plus a0, times z. When the elevator accelerates upward, the effective gravity increases from g to g plus a0, and the pressure difference between any two vertical points in the liquid increases accordingly. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A body is fully submerged in a liquid of density rho, inside an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a0. Find the buoyant force B on the body.|id=ex-q-1>> Suppose a body is fully submerged in a liquid of density rho — that's our liquid — and the elevator is going up with an upward acceleration a0. We want to find the buoyant force B acting on the body. The key idea is the substitution trick. We mentally replace the submerged body with the same volume of liquid — that is, we fill that space with the surrounding liquid. Since the whole liquid is now a homogeneous mass, this substituted portion is at rest relative to the rest of the liquid, so it accelerates upward at a0 together with everything else. <<WRITE_STEP:Substituted liquid: mass m = mass of displaced liquid, accelerating upward at a0|id=ex-step-1-1>> The substituted liquid has mass m equal to the mass of the displaced liquid, and it is moving upward with the same acceleration a0. Now let's identify the two forces acting on the substituted liquid. <<WRITE_STEP:Forces on substituted liquid: (a) Buoyant force B — upward, (b) Weight mg — downward|id=ex-step-1-2>> First, there is the buoyant force B acting upward, supplied by the surrounding liquid. Second, there is the weight m times g acting downward. These are the only two forces — there is no contact force from a solid body anymore, because we replaced that body with liquid. We apply Newton's second law to the substituted liquid. The net upward force equals m times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:Newton's second law → B − mg = m times a0|id=ex-step-1-3>> So B minus m times g equals m times a0. Rearranging, we bring m times g to the right-hand side. <<WRITE_STEP:Rearranging → B = m times g + m times a0 = m times (g + a0)|id=ex-step-1-4>> That gives us B equals m times g plus m times a0, which we factor as m times the quantity g plus a0. And there is the answer. <<WRITE_ANSWER:B = m(g + a0), where m is the mass of the displaced liquid|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> The buoyant force is B equals m times the quantity g plus a0, where m is the mass of the displaced liquid. Notice that the effective gravitational pull has been replaced by g plus a0 — so when the elevator accelerates upward, buoyancy becomes stronger than it would be at rest. The faster the upward acceleration a0, the greater the buoyant force on any submerged object. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A beaker of liquid accelerates horizontally with acceleration a0. Points A and B are at the same horizontal level, separated by distance l along the direction of acceleration. The liquid has density rho. Find the tilt angle theta of the free surface.|id=ex-q-2>> We have a beaker accelerating horizontally with acceleration a0. Points A and B sit at the same horizontal level, separated by distance l along the direction of that acceleration. The pressure at A is P1 and the pressure at B is P2, and the density of the liquid is rho. Our goal is to find how steeply the free surface tilts. We start by applying Newton's second law to a small horizontal cylinder of liquid connecting A to B. The liquid on the left pushes with force P1 times delta S toward the right, and the liquid on the right pushes back with P2 times delta S toward the left. The mass of liquid in that cylinder is delta S times l times rho. Setting net force equal to mass times acceleration we get: P1 times delta S minus P2 times delta S equals delta S times l times rho times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:(P1 − P2)ΔS = (ΔS) · l · ρ · a0|id=ex-step-2-1>> Dividing both sides by delta S, this simplifies beautifully: P1 minus P2 equals l times rho times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 − P2 = l · ρ · a0|id=ex-step-2-2>> So even though A and B are at the same horizontal level, there IS a pressure difference between them whenever the liquid accelerates horizontally. Now we bring in the depth expressions. Because there is no vertical acceleration, the usual hydrostatic rule still holds vertically. So the pressure at A is P0 plus h1 times rho times g, and the pressure at B is P0 plus h2 times rho times g, where h1 and h2 are the depths of A and B below the free surface. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 = P0 + h1·ρ·g,   P2 = P0 + h2·ρ·g|id=ex-step-2-3>> We substitute these into our earlier result P1 minus P2 equals l times rho times a0. <<WRITE_STEP:(P0 + h1·ρ·g) − (P0 + h2·ρ·g) = l·ρ·a0|id=ex-step-2-4>> The atmospheric pressure P0 cancels on both sides, and rho cancels too, leaving us with: h1 times g minus h2 times g equals l times a0. Dividing both sides by l times g gives us the slope of the free surface. <<WRITE_STEP:(h1 − h2) / l = a0 / g|id=ex-step-2-5>> Now look at what the left-hand side means geometrically: h1 minus h2 is the vertical rise across the horizontal distance l. That ratio is exactly the tangent of the angle theta that the free surface makes with the horizontal. <<WRITE_STEP:tan θ = (h1 − h2) / l = a0 / g|id=ex-step-2-6>> So the free surface tilts at an angle whose tangent equals a0 divided by g. <<WRITE_ANSWER:tan θ = a0 / g  (theta = tilt angle of the free surface)|id=ex-ans-2>> The faster the beaker accelerates, the steeper the tilt — and notice it doesn't depend on the density of the liquid or the separation l at all. <<WRITE_KEY:Buoyant force = ρV(g + a₀) in accelerating fluid|id=key-2>>That means in an upward-accelerating elevator, objects feel MORE buoyancy — they float more easily. And in free fall, a zero equals minus g, so g plus a zero equals zero, and the buoyant force vanishes entirely. That's your weightless water. <<POINT:arrow-accel>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:height-z>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Free fall: a₀ = −g → buoyancy = 0|id=text-2>>So to tie it together: whether we're talking about pressure difference between two points or the buoyant force on a submerged body, the rule is the same — swap out g for the effective gravity g plus a zero. The fluid 'forgets' that it's in an elevator; it just responds to whatever net downward pull it feels.

topics.orig_book_content:
13.7 FLOW OF FLUIDS
The flow of fluid is in general a complex branch of
mechanics. If you look at the motion of water in a fall
(like Rallah fall near Manali or Kemti fall near
Moussurie) the view is very pleasant. The water falls
from a height and then proceeds on a flat bed or a
slope with thumping, jumping and singing if you can
appreciate the music. But if you try to analyse the
motion of each particle on the basis of laws of
mechanics, the task is tremendously difficult. Other
examples of fluid flow are the sailing of clouds and the
motion of smoke when a traditional Chulha using coal,
wood or goitha (prepared from cowdung) in an Indian
village is lit. The motion of each smoke particle is
governed by the same Newton’s laws but to predict the
motion of a particular particle is not easy.
topics.our_understanding: Welcome to the section on the flow of fluids. Now, before we dive into the detailed mathematics of fluid mechanics, it is really important to appreciate just how complex and beautiful fluid flow actually is. Think about a waterfall — water tumbling down from a great height, splashing and jumping and rushing along a rocky bed. It looks almost alive, doesn't it? And in a way, that is exactly the challenge. Every single tiny droplet of water in that waterfall is obeying the same Newton's laws of motion that you have already studied. Force equals mass times acceleration. Every particle, every moment. And yet, if you tried to sit down and actually calculate the exact path of even one of those droplets — tracking every push, every splash, every collision with a rock — the mathematics becomes almost impossibly complicated. That is the honest truth about fluid mechanics, and it is worth saying out loud right at the start. The laws governing the motion are simple and familiar. The actual prediction of motion for any given particle is enormously difficult. Think about smoke rising from a fire. Each tiny smoke particle is being pushed around by air currents, gravity, heat, and the movements of neighboring particles. Again, Newton's laws apply to every one of them, but predicting where a particular smoke particle will end up is a real challenge. This section is setting the stage for you — it is telling you that fluid flow is a rich, complex, and genuinely hard area of physics. As we move forward, we will look at simplified models and special cases that make the problem manageable. We will make assumptions, like assuming the fluid flows smoothly without turbulence, and those assumptions will let us derive some beautiful and useful results. But always keep in the back of your mind that real fluid flow — the waterfall, the clouds sailing across the sky, the smoke from a village fire — is far richer and more complicated than any simple model can fully capture. That humility is actually a sign of good scientific thinking.

events.text: Each droplet: F = ma, every moment
Billions of droplets → billions of interactions
Complexity comes from interactions, not from the rules
Fluid flow: simple laws, staggering complexity

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_7:waterfall_complexity>> Every single water droplet in a waterfall perfectly obeys Newton's laws — force equals mass times acceleration, every particle, every moment. So why can't we predict where any one of them will land? <<TRACE:droplet-crowd>> <<FOCUS:single-droplet>> <<SECTION:Fluids and Newton's Laws|id=sec-1>>Let's zoom in. Take just one droplet out of that waterfall. It has a mass, gravity pulls it down, and we can write every force acting on it. Newton's laws are crystal clear here. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Each droplet: F = ma, every moment|id=text-1>>The same physics you used to calculate a ball rolling down a ramp applies right here — to this one droplet. Simple. Clean. Predictable. <<POINT:force-arrow>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now put all the droplets back together. <<TRACE:droplet-crowd>> <<FOCUS:interaction-lines>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Billions of droplets → billions of interactions|id=text-2>>Each one is bumping into its neighbours, being pushed sideways, losing speed here, gaining it there. The interactions between particles explode in number. <<TRACE:interaction-lines>> Here's the real question: if every particle is following simple, known laws — why is it so impossibly hard to work out what even one droplet will do? <<POINT:droplet-crowd>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:interaction-lines>> <<WRITE_KEY:Complexity comes from interactions, not from the rules|id=key-1>>The answer is that complexity doesn't come from the rules — it comes from the interactions. Billions of particles, each affecting every neighbour, every instant. The maths doesn't break down; it just becomes astronomically large. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> It's the same story with smoke rising from a fire. Every smoke particle obeys Newton's second law — you could write the equation for it right now. But watch smoke curl and twist and loop back on itself — that's the same equations playing out across millions of particles at once. <<PAUSE:short>> Or think about clouds drifting across the sky. Each tiny water droplet and air molecule is following the same simple rule: net force equals mass times acceleration. The grand, sweeping motion of the whole cloud emerges from uncountable tiny interactions. <<WRITE_KEY:Fluid flow: simple laws, staggering complexity|id=key-2>>So here is the big idea to hold onto: fluid mechanics is NOT about new physics. It is Newton's old laws, applied to so many particles at once that prediction becomes the challenge — not the principles. <<PAUSE:short>> This is why fluid flow is one of the richest, most beautiful — and most difficult — areas of classical mechanics. And the first step to taming it is to classify what kinds of flow are even possible. That's exactly where we go next.

topics.orig_book_content:
13.8 STEADY AND TURBULENT FLOW
Consider a liquid passing through a glass tube
(figure 13.11). Concentrate on a particular point A in
the tube and look at the particles arriving at A. If the
velocity of the liquid is small, all the particles which
come to A will have same speed and will move in same
direction. As a particle goes from A to another point
B, its speed and direction may change, but all the
particles reaching A will have the same speed at A and
all the particles reaching B will have the same speed
at B. Also, if one particle passing through A has gone
through B, then all the particles passing through A go
through B. Such a flow of fluid is called a steady flow.
In steady flow the velocity of fluid particles
reaching a particular point is the same at all time.
Thus, each particle follows the same path as taken by
a previous particle passing through that point.
If the liquid is pushed in the tube at a rapid rate,
the flow may become turbulent. In this case, the
velocities of different particles passing through the
same point may be different and change erratically
with time. The motion of water in a high fall or a fast
flowing river is, in general, turbulent.
Steady flow is also called streamline flow.
Line of Flow : Streamline
The path taken by a particle in flowing fluid is
called its line of flow. The tangent at any point on the
line of flow gives the direction of motion of that particle
at that point. In the case of steady flow, all the
particles passing through a given point follow the same
path and hence we have a unique line of flow passing
through a given point. In this case, the line of flow is
also called a streamline. Thus, the tangent to the
streamline at any point gives the direction of all the
particles passing through that point. It is clear that
two streamlines cannot intersect, otherwise, the
particle reaching at the intersection will have two
different directions of motion.
Tube of Flow
Consider an area S in a fluid in steady flow. Draw
streamlines from all the points of the periphery of S.
These streamlines enclose a tube, of which S is a cross-
section. Such a tube is called a tube of flow. As the
streamlines do not cross each other, fluid flowing
through differnt tubes of flow cannot intermix,
although there is no physical partition between the
tubes. When a liquid is passed slowly through a pipe,
the pipe itself is one tube of flow.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something you've probably noticed without realizing it — the difference between smooth, calm water flowing through a pipe and the wild, churning water of a waterfall. That difference is exactly what this section is about: steady flow versus turbulent flow.

Imagine a glass tube with liquid moving through it. Pick any single point inside that tube — let's call it point A. Now watch all the tiny particles of liquid arriving at A one after another. If the liquid is moving slowly, something beautiful happens: every single particle that arrives at A has the same speed and moves in the same direction. And if you follow one particle from A to another point B, it takes a specific path. Here's the key insight — every other particle that passes through A will follow that exact same path and arrive at B with the same speed. This is what we call steady flow, and it's also known as streamline flow. The defining idea is that the velocity at any fixed point in the fluid stays the same over time.

Now, what happens if you push the liquid through the tube much faster? The flow can become turbulent. In turbulent flow, particles arriving at the same point A might have completely different speeds and directions at different moments. Think about water crashing down a tall waterfall or rushing through a fast river — that chaotic, unpredictable motion is turbulence.

In steady flow, the path that any particle traces through the fluid is called its line of flow. The direction the particle is moving at any moment is given by the tangent to that line — imagine drawing a straight line that just touches the curve at one point, pointing in the direction of travel. In steady flow, since every particle through a given point follows the same path, we get a unique, well-defined line called a streamline. The tangent to a streamline at any point tells you the direction of motion of all particles passing through that point.

Here's a really important consequence: two streamlines can never cross each other. Think about why — if they did cross, a particle arriving at that intersection would have two different directions to go, which is impossible. One particle, one direction.

Finally, imagine drawing streamlines from every point around the edge of some small area inside the fluid. All those streamlines together form a tube-shaped region called a tube of flow. Because streamlines never cross, fluid inside one tube of flow stays inside it — it never mixes with fluid in a neighboring tube, even though there's no physical wall separating them. When liquid flows slowly through a pipe, the entire pipe acts as one big tube of flow. These ideas lay the foundation for understanding how fluids behave in a controlled, predictable way.

events.text: Steady flow → every particle through A follows the same streamline
Streamlines never cross each other
Steady flow = velocity at each point constant in time
Turbulent flow → velocity at same point changes erratically
Slow → steady (streamline). Fast → turbulent

topics.orig_book_content:
13.9 IRROTATIONAL FLOW OF AN
     INCOMPRESSIBLE AND NONVISCOUS FLUID
The analysis of the flow of a fluid becomes much
simplified if we consider the fluid to be incompressible
and nonviscous and that the flow is irrotational.
Incompressibility means that the density of the fluid
is same at all the points and remains constant as time
passes. This assumption is quite good for liquids and
is valid in certain cases of flow of gases. Viscosity of
a fluid is related to the internal friction when a layer
of fluid slips over another layer. Mechanical energy is
lost against such viscous forces. The assumption of a
nonviscous fluid will mean that we are neglecting the
effect of such internal friction. Irrotational flow means
there is no net angular velocity of fluid particles. When
you put some washing powder in a bucket containing
water and mix it by rotating your hand in circular
path along the wall of the bucket, the water comes into
rotational motion. Quite often water flowing in rivers
show small vortex formation where it goes in rotational
motion about a centre.  Now onwards we shall consider
only the irrotational motion of an incompressible and
nonviscous fluid.
topics.our_understanding:
Alright, let's talk about a very important set of simplifying assumptions that physicists and engineers use when studying how fluids move. This section introduces us to a special kind of fluid flow — one that is irrotational, incompressible, and nonviscous. These three words might sound intimidating, but each one is actually a pretty straightforward idea, and together they make the mathematics of fluid flow much, much easier to handle.

Let's start with incompressibility. When we say a fluid is incompressible, we mean its density stays the same everywhere and at all times. Think about water — no matter how hard you push on it, it doesn't really squish down and become denser. That's what incompressibility captures. This assumption works really well for liquids, and it even holds up in certain situations involving gases.

Next, nonviscous. Viscosity is basically the internal friction inside a fluid. Imagine honey flowing compared to water — honey is much more viscous because its layers resist sliding past each other, and that resistance eats up mechanical energy. When we assume a fluid is nonviscous, we're saying we're going to ignore that internal friction. It's a simplification, yes, but it's a very useful one that lets us focus on the big picture of how the fluid moves.

Now, irrotational flow is perhaps the most interesting of the three. This means that the fluid particles themselves have no net spinning or rotating motion as they travel. To picture the opposite — rotational flow — think about stirring water in a bucket by moving your hand in circles along the wall. The water starts spinning around a central point. Or think about those little whirlpools, called vortices, that you sometimes see in rivers. That swirling, spinning motion is exactly what we are ruling out when we say the flow is irrotational.

So why do we bother with all these assumptions? Because when you combine all three — incompressible, nonviscous, and irrotational — the equations describing the fluid become dramatically simpler and solvable. This is the foundation for a beautiful and powerful branch of fluid mechanics. From here on, everything we study in this topic will be built on these three pillars.

events.text: Assumption 1 — Incompressible: density same everywhere, always
Assumption 2 — Nonviscous: no internal friction
Assumption 3 — Irrotational: no particle spins about its own axis
Irrotational ≠ straight-line flow. It means no individual particle self-spins.
Ideal fluid = incompressible + nonviscous + irrotational → no energy loss, maths stays clean.

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_9:fluid_assumptions>> When you stir water in a bucket, every little bit of water spins around. But rivers can flow smoothly for kilometres without a single whirlpool. What's the difference — and why does it matter so much to engineers? <<TRACE:bucket-vortex>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:The Three Magic Assumptions|id=sec-1>>To make the maths of flowing fluids manageable, physicists zero in on a special kind of fluid — one that satisfies three clean assumptions. Let's build each one from scratch. <<FOCUS:density-dots-uniform>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Assumption 1 — Incompressible: density same everywhere, always|id=text-1>>First: incompressibility. Push water as hard as you like — it refuses to squish. Its density stays the same at every point and at every moment. Liquids are almost always like this. <<FOCUS:viscous-layers>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Assumption 2 — Nonviscous: no internal friction|id=text-2>>Second: nonviscosity. Real fluids have layers that slide over each other, and that sliding creates internal friction — a bit like rubbing your hands together. Energy gets lost as heat. <<FOCUS:nonviscous-layers>> A nonviscous fluid simply ignores that friction. One layer glides past the next with zero resistance — no energy wasted. Water and air, at everyday speeds, are remarkably close to this ideal. <<FOCUS:irrotational-particle>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Assumption 3 — Irrotational: no particle spins about its own axis|id=text-3>>Third — and this is the trickiest one. Irrotational. Here's the question: can a fluid particle travel along a curved path WITHOUT spinning about its own centre? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:irrotational-particle>> Absolutely yes. Think of a car going around a roundabout — the car follows a curved road, but the car itself isn't rolling sideways. Irrotational means each tiny blob of fluid has zero net rotation about its own axis, even as the whole flow curves. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:bucket-vortex>> <<WRITE_KEY:Irrotational ≠ straight-line flow. It means no individual particle self-spins.|id=key-1>>Compare it to rotational flow — stir a bucket and you create a vortex. Every particle of water is literally spinning about a central axis. That's rotational flow, and it makes the equations far harder. <<TRACE:bucket-vortex>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:river-streamlines>> A smooth river, away from eddies, is the opposite: the water moves forward, follows bends, but no particle tumbles about itself. That's irrotational flow in the real world. <<TRACE:river-streamlines>> So now put all three together. Incompressible: density is locked. Nonviscous: no energy lost to friction. Irrotational: no particle self-spins. A fluid that ticks all three boxes is called an ideal fluid. <<POINT:nonviscous-layers>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ideal fluid = incompressible + nonviscous + irrotational → no energy loss, maths stays clean.|id=key-2>>Here's why this matters: an ideal fluid flowing through any pipe or channel conserves all of its mechanical energy. Nothing leaks away. That single fact unlocks the beautiful equations we'll use from here on. <<POINT:density-dots-uniform>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Is the ideal fluid real? Not perfectly — no fluid is truly frictionless. But water, air, and many gases behave close enough that the ideal-fluid predictions match experiments to within a few percent. That's why every engineer learns this model first. So the next time you see water flowing calmly in a channel — no whirlpools, no churning — you're looking at something very close to our ideal fluid: incompressible, nonviscous, and irrotational. Those three words are the passport to all the elegant fluid physics ahead. <<TRACE:river-streamlines>> <<PAUSE:short>>

13.10 EQUATION OF CONTINUITY
We have seen that the fluid going through a tube
of flow does not intermix with fluid in other tubes. The
total mass of fluid going into the tube through any
cross section should, therefore, be equal to the total
mass coming out of the same tube from any other cross
section in the same time. This leads to the equation
of continuity.
Let us consider two cross sections of a tube of flow
at the points A and B (figure 13.13). Let the area of
cross section at A be A1 and that at B be A2. Let the
speed of the fluid be v1 at A and v2 at B.
How much fluid goes into the tube through the

construct a cylinder of length v1∆t at A as shown in
the figure. As the fluid at A has speed v1, all the fluid
included in this cylinder will cross through A1 in the

into the tube through the cross section at A is
A1v1∆t. Similarly, the volume of the fluid going out of
the tube through the cross section at B is A2v2∆t. If
the fluid is incompressible, we must have

topics.our_understanding:
Imagine water flowing through a garden hose. Now picture squeezing one end of that hose — the water shoots out faster from the narrow part, right? That's exactly what the equation of continuity is all about, and today we're going to understand why that happens from first principles.

The key idea starts with something very simple: fluid flowing through a tube of flow doesn't mix with fluid in neighboring tubes. Think of the flow as a collection of separate invisible pipes, each carrying its own stream. Because of this, whatever mass of fluid enters one end of a tube must come out the other end in the same amount of time. The fluid can't just disappear or pile up inside — that would violate conservation of mass.

Now let's think carefully about how much fluid passes through a cross section in a short time interval. Say the fluid is moving at speed v at a particular cross section with area A. In a tiny time interval, the fluid travels a distance of v times that interval. So the volume that passes through is area times that distance, which gives us A times v times the time interval. That's the volume flowing past any cross section per unit time.

Now apply this to two different points along the same tube — call them point A and point B. At point A, the cross-sectional area is A one and the speed is v one. At point B, the area is A two and the speed is v two. Since the fluid is incompressible — meaning it can't be squeezed into a smaller volume — the volume flowing in at A must equal the volume flowing out at B in the same time. This gives us A one times v one equals A two times v two. This beautiful relationship is the equation of continuity.

What it tells you is that the product of area and speed stays constant all along a tube of flow. So if the tube gets narrower, the area goes down, and the speed must go up to compensate. If the tube widens, the speed drops. This is why water speeds up when you put your thumb over a hose nozzle — you're reducing the area, so the speed has to increase to keep that product constant. We'll look at a diagram in a moment that makes this very visual.

This equation is really just conservation of mass dressed up in the language of fluid flow. It's one of the most powerful and elegant ideas in all of fluid mechanics, and once you see it, you'll notice it everywhere — in rivers, blood vessels, ventilation systems, and more.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the most beautiful and powerful ideas in all of fluid mechanics — the Bernoulli equation. At its heart, this equation is simply the work-energy theorem applied to a flowing liquid. It connects three things at any point in a flowing fluid: the pressure at that point, the speed of the fluid there, and the height of that point above some reference level.

Here's the setup to keep in mind. Imagine a liquid flowing smoothly through a pipe that changes both its width and its height as it goes — like a garden hose that narrows at one end and curves upward. We assume the liquid is incompressible, meaning it doesn't squish, and nonviscous, meaning there's no internal friction. The flow is also steady, so the speed at any fixed point in the pipe doesn't change over time.

Now, think about a chunk of liquid sitting between two cross sections of this pipe, which we'll call A and B. After a tiny time interval, that chunk shifts forward a little. The liquid behind it pushes it forward with a force equal to pressure times area at A, and the liquid ahead of it pushes back with a force equal to pressure times area at B. Gravity also does work on it as it moves up or down. The walls of the pipe push on the liquid too, but since that force is always perpendicular to the motion, it does zero work.

When we carefully add up all the work done — by the pressure forces and by gravity — and set that equal to the change in kinetic energy of the liquid, something wonderful happens. After dividing through by the mass element, we get a clean result: pressure divided by density, plus g times height, plus one half times v squared, is the same at every point along the flow. Multiplying through by density gives us the classic form: pressure plus rho times g times h plus one half times rho times v squared equals a constant throughout the fluid.

What this tells you is deeply intuitive once you see it. If the pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up — you already know that from the continuity equation. But now Bernoulli tells you that when the speed goes up, the pressure must go down to keep that sum constant. Faster flow means lower pressure. This single insight explains how airplane wings generate lift, how a spray bottle works, and why a shower curtain gets pulled inward. It's one of those ideas that keeps showing up everywhere once you know it.

Figure (13.16) shows a liquid of density 1200 kg m−3 flowing steadily in a tube of varying cross section. The cross section at a point A is 1.0 cm2 and that at B is 20 mm2, the points A and B are in the same horizontal plane. The speed of the liquid at A is 10 cm s–1. Calculate the difference in pressures at A and B.

Solution : From equation of continuity, the speed v2 at B is given by,
                 A1v1 = A2v2
or,           (1.0 cm2) (10 cm s−1) = (20 mm2)v2
or,     v2 = 1.0 cm2 / 20 mm2 × 10 cm s−1 = 50 cm s−1 .
By Bernoulli equation,
      P1 + ρgh1 + 1/2 ρv12 = P2 + ρgh2 + 1/2 ρv22 .
Here h1 = h2. Thus,
P1 − P2 = 1/2 ρv22 − 1/2 ρv12 
= 1/2 × (1200 kg m−3) (2500 cm2 s−2 − 100 cm2 s−2)
= 600 kg m−3 × 2400 cm2 s−2 = 144 Pa.

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> Here's something that will mess with your head: the faster a fluid flows, the LOWER its pressure. Speed up — pressure drops. Slow down — pressure rises. That feels completely backwards. But it's the reason aeroplanes fly, and it's all hiding inside one beautiful equation. <<FOCUS:pipe-wide-section>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:fluid_mechanics:13_11:bernoulli_pipe>> <<SECTION:Setup — the pipe|id=sec-1>>You already know the equation of continuity: when a pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up to keep the same volume flowing every second. Now let's ask a deeper question — what happens to the PRESSURE when that happens? <<FOCUS:pipe-wide-section>> Picture this pipe — wide and low on the left, narrow and high on the right. Fluid is flowing steadily; it's incompressible, so nothing squishes; and there's no friction slowing it down. At the wide end, call the area A one, the speed v one, the pressure P one, and the height h one. <<POINT:pipe-wide-section>> <<FOCUS:pipe-narrow-section>> At the narrow end: area A two, speed v two, pressure P two, height h two. <<POINT:pipe-narrow-section>> <<FOCUS:fluid-element-A>> <<SECTION:Work done by pressure forces|id=sec-2>>Now let's track a small chunk of fluid — mass delta m — as it shifts from the wide section to the narrow one. Two pressure forces do work on it: the pressure behind it at the inlet PUSHES it forward, and the pressure ahead at the outlet PUSHES BACK. <<TRACE:fluid-element-A>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrow-P1>> The force at the inlet is P one times A one, and it pushes the chunk through a small distance v one times delta t. So the work done BY the inlet pressure is P one times A one times v one times delta t. <<POINT:pressure-arrow-P1>> <<FOCUS:pressure-arrow-P2>> At the outlet, the pressure P two pushes BACK on the chunk over distance v two times delta t — that's negative work: minus P two times A two times v two times delta t. <<WRITE_STEP:Net work = (P1 − P2) × Δm/ρ|id=step-1>> <<POINT:pressure-arrow-P2>> <<FOCUS:fluid-element-B>> <<SECTION:Energy changes|id=sec-3>>By continuity, A one v one equals A two v two, so the volumes are equal and the mass delta m is the same at both ends. The net work by pressure then simplifies to the pressure DIFFERENCE times delta m divided by rho — that's the energy the pressure forces put in. Now, where does that energy GO? The work-energy theorem says it goes into two places: the change in kinetic energy of the chunk, and the change in its gravitational potential energy as it climbs from h one to h two. <<WRITE_STEP:W_pressure = ΔKE + ΔPE|id=step-2>> <<POINT:height-h2>> <<POINT:height-h2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:ΔKE = ½Δm(v₂² − v₁²), ΔPE = Δmg(h₂ − h₁)|id=step-3>>The kinetic energy change is one-half delta m times open bracket v two squared minus v one squared close bracket. The potential energy change is delta m times g times open bracket h two minus h one close bracket. Setting pressure work equal to the sum of these two, and dividing through by the volume delta m over rho, every term becomes energy per unit volume. <<PAUSE:short>> Each term is energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy — and their sum never changes along the flow. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> And when we rearrange, everything from side one equals everything from side two: P one plus one-half rho v one squared plus rho g h one equals P two plus one-half rho v two squared plus rho g h two. <<WRITE_KEY:P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> We can write this more compactly: at any point in the fluid, pressure plus one-half rho v squared plus rho g h equals the same constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}|id=eq-2|boxed>> That's Bernoulli's equation — and notice what it IS: it's the work-energy theorem wearing fluid-mechanics clothes. Each term is energy per unit volume. Pressure energy, kinetic energy, potential energy — they shift between each other, but their SUM stays constant. <<POINT:pipe-narrow-section>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A liquid of density one thousand two hundred kilograms per cubic meter flows steadily through a tube. The cross-sectional area at point A is one point zero square centimeters, and at point B it is twenty square millimeters. Points A and B are at the same horizontal height. The speed at A is ten centimeters per second. Find the difference in pressures at A and B.|id=ex-q-1>> We have a liquid of density one thousand two hundred kilograms per cubic meter, the cross-sectional area at A is one point zero square centimeters, and the cross-sectional area at B is twenty square millimeters. Points A and B are at the same horizontal height, so h one equals h two, and the speed of the liquid at A is ten centimeters per second. Our goal is to find the pressure difference P one minus P two. We start with the continuity equation to find the speed at B, because Bernoulli's equation will need both speeds. The continuity equation says A one times v one equals A two times v two. <<WRITE_STEP:Continuity: A1·v1 = A2·v2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Substituting in our values, one point zero square centimeters times ten centimeters per second equals twenty square millimeters times v two. <<WRITE_STEP:(1.0 cm²)(10 cm/s) = (20 mm²) · v2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Since one point zero square centimeters equals one hundred square millimeters, we get v two equals one hundred square millimeters times ten centimeters per second, all divided by twenty square millimeters. <<PAUSE:short>> That gives us v two equals fifty centimeters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:v2 = (100 mm² × 10 cm/s) ÷ 20 mm² = 50 cm/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> So the speed at B found from the continuity equation is fifty centimeters per second. Now we apply Bernoulli's equation. The full form is P one plus rho g h one plus one half rho v one squared equals P two plus rho g h two plus one half rho v two squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 + ρgh1 + ½ρv1² = P2 + ρgh2 + ½ρv2²|id=ex-step-1-4>> Because points A and B are at the same horizontal height, h one equals h two, so those gravity terms cancel. Rearranging, we get P one minus P two equals one half rho v two squared minus one half rho v one squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Since h1 = h2 → P1 − P2 = ½ρ(v2² − v1²)|id=ex-step-1-5>> Let's now substitute the numbers. v two squared is fifty centimeters per second squared, which is two thousand five hundred square centimeters per second squared. And v one squared is ten centimeters per second squared, which is one hundred square centimeters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:v2² = 2500 cm²/s²,  v1² = 100 cm²/s²|id=ex-step-1-6>> So P one minus P two equals one half times one thousand two hundred kilograms per cubic meter times the quantity two thousand five hundred minus one hundred square centimeters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P1 − P2 = ½ × 1200 kg/m³ × (2500 − 100) cm²/s²|id=ex-step-1-7>> That simplifies to six hundred kilograms per cubic meter times two thousand four hundred square centimeters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:= 600 kg/m³ × 2400 cm²/s²|id=ex-step-1-8>> Converting square centimeters per second squared to SI units and multiplying through, the pressure difference P one minus P two equals one hundred forty-four pascals. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:P1 − P2 = 144 pascals|id=ex-ans-1>> So the liquid at the narrower point B is moving faster — fifty centimeters per second compared to ten centimeters per second at A — and as Bernoulli's equation tells us, that higher speed comes with a lower pressure, giving us a pressure difference of one hundred forty-four pascals. <<FOCUS:pipe-narrow-section>> <<SECTION:The paradox resolved|id=sec-4>>So now — back to the paradox from the start. Imagine a HORIZONTAL pipe: h one equals h two, so the height terms cancel. The equation becomes P one plus one-half rho v one squared equals P two plus one-half rho v two squared. If the pipe narrows and v two is bigger than v one — what must happen to P two? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Exactly — P two must be SMALLER. The kinetic energy term one-half rho v squared grew because the fluid sped up, so the pressure term P has to SHRINK to keep the total constant. <<WRITE_KEY:Faster flow → lower pressure|id=key-2>>Speed up, pressure drops. (c) Ventury Tube
A ventury tube is used to measure the flow speed
of a fluid in a tube. It consists of a constriction or a
throat in the tube. As the fluid passes through the
constriction, its speed increases in accordance with the
equation of continuity. The pressure thus decreases as
required by Bernoulli equation.

(d) Aspirator Pump
When a fluid passes through a region at a large
speed, the pressure there decreases. This fact finds a
number of useful applications. In an aspirator pump a
barrel A terminates in a small constriction B (figure
13.19). A narrow tube C connects the constriction to a
vessel containing the liquid to be sprayed. The air in
the barrel A is pushed by the operator through a
piston. As the air passes through the constriction B,
its speed is considerably increased and consequently
the pressure drops. Due to reduced pressure in the
constriction B, the liquid is raised from the vessel and
is sprayed with the expelled air.
(e) Change of Plane of Motion of a Spinning Ball
Quite often when swing bowlers of cricket deliver
the ball, the ball changes its plane of motion in air.
Such a deflection from the plane of projection may be
explained on the basis of Bernoulli equation.
Suppose a ball spinning about the vertical direction
is going ahead with some velocity in the horizontal
direction in otherwise still air. Let us work in a frame
in which the centre of the ball is at rest. In this frame
the air moves past the ball at a speed v in the opposite
direction. The situation is shown in (13.20).
The plane of the figure represents horizontal plane.
The air that goes from the A side of the ball in the
figure is dragged by the spin of the ball and its speed
increases. The air that goes from the B side of the ball
in the figure suffers an opposite drag and its speed
decreases. The pressure of air is reduced on the A side
and is increased on the B side as required by the
Bernoulli’s theorem. As a result, a net force F acts on
the ball from the B side to the A side due to this
pressure difference. This force causes the deviation of
the plane of motion.

are heavier than the molecules of a lighter liquid ?

you are hurt. But if someone presses a rod against your

topics.our_understanding:
Welcome to one of the most satisfying parts of fluid mechanics — actually using Bernoulli's equation to explain real things happening in the world around you. Let's walk through the big ideas together.

First, notice something elegant: if you set the speed of a fluid to zero everywhere in Bernoulli's equation, you get back the hydrostatics result you already know. Pressure increases as you go deeper. That's a nice sanity check — Bernoulli's equation contains hydrostatics as a special case.

Now the really exciting stuff. Imagine a large tank of water with a small hole near the bottom. The water level is a height h above the hole. Because the tank is so much wider than the hole, the water at the top barely moves compared to the water shooting out. When you apply Bernoulli's equation and the continuity equation together, and use the fact that both the top surface and the hole are open to the atmosphere, the math simplifies beautifully. The speed of water coming out equals the square root of two times g times h. This is called Torricelli's theorem, and here's the stunning part — that speed is exactly the same as the speed a ball would reach if you dropped it from height h under gravity. The hole in the tank and a falling ball are governed by the same physics.

Next, think about a Venturi tube. This is a pipe that narrows in the middle. As fluid enters the narrow section, it must speed up — the continuity equation demands it, because the same volume of fluid has to squeeze through a smaller opening every second. And when speed goes up, Bernoulli tells us pressure must come down. By measuring the pressure difference between the wide and narrow sections — which you can read off the heights of liquid in two vertical tubes connected to the pipe — you can calculate exactly how fast the fluid is flowing. This is how engineers measure flow rates in pipes.

The aspirator pump works on the same idea. Air is pushed through a narrow constriction, its speed shoots up, and the pressure drops. That low pressure region sucks liquid up from a container below and sprays it out with the air. Think of a perfume atomizer or a paint sprayer.

Finally, consider a spinning cricket ball moving through the air. On one side, the spin drags air along with the ball, adding to the air's speed. On the other side, the spin works against the airflow, slowing it down. Faster air means lower pressure on one side, slower air means higher pressure on the other side. That pressure difference pushes the ball sideways, curving its path. This is why a skilled swing bowler can make the ball curve in the air — pure Bernoulli in action on the cricket field.

These applications all share one core idea: in a moving fluid, where speed is high, pressure is low, and where speed is low, pressure is high. Once you truly own that idea, you can explain everything from water tanks to spinning balls.

Example 13.5
A water tank is constructed on the top of a building. With what speed will the water come out of a tap 6.0 m below the water level in the tank? Assume steady flow and that the pressure above the water level is equal to the atmospheric pressure.
Solution: The velocity is given by Torricelli's theorem
v = √(2gh)
= √(2 × (9.8 m s−2) × (6.0 m)) ≈ 11 m s−1.
book_examples.lesson_focus: Torricelli's theorem lets you find the speed of water leaving a tank by treating it like a free-fall problem over the same height.
