book_examples.verbatim_text:
Worked Out Example 10. Water flows in a horizontal tube as shown in figure (13-W6). The pressure of water changes by 600 N m−2 between A and B where the areas of cross section are 30 cm2 and 15 cm2 respectively. Find the rate of flow of water through the tube.
Solution: Let the velocity at A = vA and that at B = vB.
By the equation of continuity, vB/vA = 30 cm2 / 15 cm2 = 2.
By Bernoulli equation,
PA + 1/2 ρ vA2 = PB + 1/2 ρ vB2
or, PA − PB = 1/2 ρ(2vA)2 − 1/2 ρ vA2 = 3/2 ρ vA2,
or, 600 N m−2 = 3/2 × (1000 kg m−3) × vA2
or, vA = √(0.4 m2 s−2) = 0.63 m s−1.
The rate of flow = 30 cm2 × 0.63 m s−1 = 1890 cm3 s−1.
book_examples.lesson_focus: By combining the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation, a measured pressure difference between two cross sections lets you calculate the actual flow rate through a tube.

velocity at B is twice the velocity at A from continuity
velocity at A works out to approximately zero point six three meters per second
rate of flow is one thousand eight hundred ninety cubic centimeters per second

book_examples.verbatim_text:
Worked Out Example 11. The area of cross section of a large tank is 0.5 m2. It has an opening near the bottom having area of cross section 1 cm2. A load of 20 kg is applied on the water at the top. Find the velocity of the water coming out of the opening at the time when the height of water level is 50 cm above the bottom. Take g = 10 m s−2.
Solution: As the area of cross section of the tank is large compared to that of the opening, the speed of water in the tank will be very small as compared to the speed at the opening. The pressure at the surface of water in the tank is that due to the atmosphere plus due to the load.
PA = P0 + (20 kg × 10 m s−2) / (0.5 m2) = P0 + 400 N m−2.
At the opening, the pressure is that due to the atmosphere.
Using Bernoulli equation:
PA + ρgh + 1/2 ρ vA2 = PB + 1/2 ρ vB2
or, P0 + 400 N m−2 + (1000 kg m−3)(10 m s−2)(0.5 m) + 0 = P0 + 1/2 × (1000 kg m−3) × vB2
or, 5400 N m−2 = 500 kg m−3 × vB2
or, vB = 3.3 m s−1.
book_examples.lesson_focus: When an extra load presses down on the water surface, it adds to the effective pressure driving the water out, so you must include that extra pressure term in Bernoulli's equation alongside the gravitational height term.

Let's see why. <<SECTION:Setting Up the Tank|id=sec-1>>Here's our setup. A tall tank, open at the top, with a small hole near the bottom. The water surface is at a height h above the hole. Those two pressure terms cancel out of Bernoulli's equation straight away. <<POINT:top-surface>> <<POINT:top-surface>> <<FOCUS:v1-arrow>> The tank is much, much wider than the hole. By the continuity equation — area times speed is constant — the top surface crawls downward almost imperceptibly compared to the jet at the hole. So we can set v one to essentially zero. <<POINT:v1-arrow>> <<FOCUS:height-h-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:v1 ≈ 0 since tank area >> hole area|id=text-2>>That leaves only two terms in Bernoulli's equation: the potential energy term rho g h on the left, and the kinetic energy term one half rho v two squared on the right. So think about what Bernoulli is telling us: all that height — all that stored gravitational energy per unit volume — gets converted entirely into kinetic energy at the hole. The fluid trades altitude for speed, one-for-one. <<TRACE:height-h-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> All the gravitational potential energy per unit volume, rho g h, converts completely into kinetic energy one half rho v two squared. Solving for v two gives us the efflux speed. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v_2 = \sqrt{2gh}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:v2-arrow>> <<WRITE_STEP:ρgh = ½ρv₂² → v₂ = √(2gh)|id=step-1>>And when you solve for v two, you get v two equals the square root of two g h. No tank width. No water density. Just the height. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:freefall-path>> Now here's the question that makes this unforgettable: does that formula look familiar to you? Think back to kinematics — what speed does a ball reach after falling freely through a height h? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torricelli's Theorem: v = √(2gh) — same as free fall!|id=key-1>>Exactly the same answer — v equals the square root of two g h. A ball in free fall and water shooting from a hole reach identical speeds over the same vertical drop. This beautiful result is called Torricelli's theorem. <<TRACE:freefall-path>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Hydrostatics as a Special Case|id=sec-2>>Before we move on, here's an elegant sanity check: what if the fluid isn't moving at all? Set both v one and v two to zero in Bernoulli's equation. <<WRITE_STEP:v=0 everywhere → P1 + ρgh1 = P2 + ρgh2|id=step-2>>The kinetic energy terms vanish, and you're left with P one plus rho g h one equals P two plus rho g h two. Rearranging: the pressure difference equals rho g times the difference in height. That's exactly the hydrostatics result you already know. <<PAUSE:short>> When fluid speed is zero everywhere, the kinetic terms drop out of Bernoulli's equation and we recover the familiar hydrostatics pressure-depth relationship. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P_1 - P_2 = \rho g (h_2 - h_1)|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A water tank sits on top of a building. With what speed does water come out of a tap six point zero meters below the water level in the tank? Assume steady flow, and that the pressure above the water level equals atmospheric pressure.|id=ex-q-1>> A water tank is constructed on top of a building. The tap is six point zero meters below the water surface. We're told the flow is steady, and that the pressure above the water level is equal to the atmospheric pressure — so Torricelli's theorem applies directly. Torricelli's theorem tells us the exit speed is the same as the speed an object would reach falling freely through the same height h. The formula is v equals the square root of two times g times h. <<WRITE_STEP:v = √(2 × g × h)|id=ex-step-1-1>> We substitute g equals nine point eight meters per second squared and h equals six point zero meters. <<WRITE_STEP:v = √(2 × 9.8 m/s² × 6.0 m)|id=ex-step-1-2>> That gives us the square root of one hundred seventeen point six meters squared per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:v = √(117.6 m²/s²)|id=ex-step-1-3>> Taking the square root, we get approximately eleven meters per second. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:v ≈ 11 m/s (approximately eleven meters per second)|id=ex-ans-1>> So the water shoots out of that tap at approximately eleven meters per second — exactly what you'd expect from a free-fall drop of six meters, which is a neat way to think about it. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Water flows through a horizontal tube. The pressure difference between points A and B is six hundred newtons per meter squared. The cross-sectional area at A is thirty centimeters squared and at B is fifteen centimeters squared. Find the rate of flow of water. (Density of water = one thousand kilograms per meter cubed.)|id=ex-q-1>> Water is flowing through a horizontal tube — so there's no height difference to worry about — and we're told the pressure drops by six hundred newtons per meter squared between the wider section A and the narrower section B. We want to find how much water, in volume per second, is passing through. We start with the continuity equation. Because the tube is horizontal and water is incompressible, the flow rate is the same everywhere, so area times velocity is constant. The cross-sectional area at A is thirty centimeters squared and at B is fifteen centimeters squared — B is exactly half the area of A — so v B divided by v A equals thirty over fifteen, which equals two. <<WRITE_STEP:Continuity: v_B / v_A = 30 cm² / 15 cm² = 2  →  v_B = 2 v_A|id=ex-step-1-1>> In other words, the velocity at B is twice the velocity at A. That's our first key result. Now we apply Bernoulli's equation. Because the tube is horizontal, the gravitational potential terms cancel, and we're left with: P A plus one half rho v A squared equals P B plus one half rho v B squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Bernoulli (horizontal): P_A + ½ρv_A² = P_B + ½ρv_B²|id=ex-step-1-2>> Rearranging, P A minus P B equals one half rho v B squared minus one half rho v A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A − P_B = ½ρ(v_B² − v_A²)|id=ex-step-1-3>> We substitute v B equals two v A, so v B squared is four v A squared, and the right-hand side becomes one half rho times four v A squared minus one half rho v A squared, which simplifies to three halves rho v A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:= ½ρ(2v_A)² − ½ρv_A² = (3/2)ρv_A²|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now we plug in the numbers. The pressure difference is six hundred newtons per meter squared, and the density of water is one thousand kilograms per meter cubed. So six hundred equals three halves times one thousand times v A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:600 N/m² = (3/2) × 1000 kg/m³ × v_A²|id=ex-step-1-5>> Solving for v A squared gives us zero point four meters squared per second squared, so v A equals the square root of zero point four, which is approximately zero point six three meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:v_A² = 600 / 1500 = 0.4 m²/s²  →  v_A = √0.4 ≈ 0.63 m/s|id=ex-step-1-6>> Finally, the rate of flow is simply the area at A multiplied by the velocity at A. That's thirty centimeters squared times zero point six three meters per second. Converting consistently, this gives us one thousand eight hundred ninety cubic centimeters per second. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Rate of flow = 30 cm² × 0.63 m/s ≈ 1890 cm³/s|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> So by combining the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation, the measured pressure difference of six hundred newtons per meter squared was enough to tell us the full flow rate: one thousand eight hundred ninety cubic centimeters per second. Here's an example from the chapter. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A tank has a cross-sectional area of zero point five meters squared and a small opening near the bottom with area one centimeter squared. A load of twenty kilograms sits on the water surface. The water level is fifty centimeters above the opening. Find the exit velocity of the water. Take g as ten meters per second squared.|id=ex-q-1>> A large tank has a cross-sectional area of zero point five meters squared, and a small opening near the bottom with a cross-sectional area of just one centimeter squared. A twenty kilogram load rests on the water surface, and the water height above the opening is fifty centimeters — that's zero point five meters. We're asked to find the speed of water coming out of the opening. Because the tank's cross-sectional area is so much larger than the opening, the speed of water inside the tank is negligible — we treat it as zero. Now, the pressure at the water surface isn't just atmospheric. The twenty kilogram load adds extra pressure. We calculate that as: force divided by area, which is twenty kilograms times ten meters per second squared, all divided by zero point five meters squared. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A = P₀ + (20 kg × 10 m/s²) / (0.5 m²)|id=ex-step-1-1>> That gives us an extra four hundred newtons per meter squared on top of atmospheric pressure. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A = P₀ + 400 N/m²|id=ex-step-1-2>> At the opening at the bottom, the pressure is simply atmospheric — P zero. Now we apply Bernoulli's equation between the water surface — point A — and the opening — point B. <<WRITE_STEP:P_A + ρgh + ½ρv_A² = P_B + ½ρv_B²|id=ex-step-1-3>> We substitute in: P A is P zero plus four hundred newtons per meter squared, the density of water is one thousand kilograms per meter cubed, g is ten meters per second squared, h is zero point five meters, and the speed at the surface v A is approximately zero. At the opening, P B is just P zero. <<WRITE_STEP:(P₀ + 400) + (1000)(10)(0.5) + 0 = P₀ + ½ × 1000 × v_B²|id=ex-step-1-4>> The P zero terms cancel from both sides, leaving us with four hundred plus five thousand — that's a total effective pressure of five thousand four hundred newtons per meter squared — equal to five hundred kilograms per meter cubed times v B squared. <<WRITE_STEP:5400 N/m² = 500 kg/m³ × v_B²|id=ex-step-1-5>> Solving for v B, we divide five thousand four hundred by five hundred to get v B squared equals ten point eight meters squared per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:v_B² = 5400 / 500 = 10.8 m²/s²|id=ex-step-1-6>> Taking the square root gives us the exit velocity. <<PAUSE:short>> And the answer is: the water exits at approximately three point three meters per second. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v_B ≈ 3.3 meters per second|id=ex-ans-1>> Notice how the twenty kilogram load contributed four hundred newtons per meter squared of extra pressure, which — on top of the gravitational term of five thousand newtons per meter squared from the water column — drove the total effective pressure up to five thousand four hundred newtons per meter squared, giving a faster exit speed than if there were no load at all. <<WRITE_KEY:Bernoulli → hydrostatics when v = 0 everywhere|id=key-2>>So Bernoulli's equation isn't separate from hydrostatics — hydrostatics is just Bernoulli's equation in disguise, for the special case when everything is still. One equation, two worlds. <<PAUSE:short>> So the two big ideas to lock in: first, when fluid flows, potential energy converts to kinetic energy, giving us the efflux speed of root two g h — identical to free fall. Second, when nothing flows, that same equation quietly becomes the pressure-depth rule of hydrostatics. Bernoulli is the master equation that contains both.

questions.q_text: A barometer shows a mercury column height of seventy-six centimeters. Using the density of mercury as thirteen thousand six hundred kilograms per cubic meter and g as nine point eight meters per second squared, calculate the atmospheric pressure in pascals. Show your full reasoning.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the principle. In a barometer, the atmospheric pressure equals the pressure exerted by the mercury column at the base of the tube. Using the pressure-depth formula: Pressure equals density times g times height.

Step 2 — Convert the height to meters. Seventy-six centimeters equals zero point seven six meters.

Step 3 — Substitute the values. Pressure equals thirteen thousand six hundred times nine point eight times zero point seven six.

Step 4 — Multiply step by step. Thirteen thousand six hundred times nine point eight equals one hundred thirty three thousand two hundred and eighty. Then one hundred thirty three thousand two hundred and eighty times zero point seven six equals one hundred and one thousand two hundred and ninety two point eight pascals.

Step 5 — Express the result. This is approximately one point zero one times ten to the power five pascals, which is defined as one standard atmosphere of pressure.

questions.q_text: Two points, A and B, are located at the same depth inside a large connected tank of water. Point A is near the left wall and point B is near the right wall. Which statement is correct?
options: A. The pressure at A is greater because it is closer to the inlet pipe
B. The pressure at B is greater because fluids always flow from left to right
C. The pressures at A and B are equal because they are at the same height in a connected fluid
D. The pressures can only be equal if the tank is perfectly cylindrical

questions.q_text: You place a tiny flat patch inside a tank of still water and measure the pressure on it. You then tilt the patch to a completely different angle at the same point. What happens to the pressure value?
options: A. It increases because the patch now faces a different direction
B. It decreases because less fluid weight acts on the tilted surface
C. It stays exactly the same because pressure at a point in a nonviscous fluid is independent of orientation
D. It changes only if you tilt the patch past 45 degrees

questions.q_text: A storage tank holds oil with a density of 800 kilograms per cubic meter. Point X is 3 meters below the oil surface and point Y is 8 meters below the oil surface. Taking g as 10 meters per second squared, find the pressure difference between point Y and point X, and explain which point has higher pressure and why.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify what we need. We want the difference in pressure between point Y (deeper) and point X (shallower). The formula for pressure difference between two depths in a fluid of constant density is: pressure difference equals density times g times the vertical distance between the two points.

Step 2 — Find the vertical distance. Point X is 3 meters below the surface and point Y is 8 meters below the surface. The vertical distance between them is 8 minus 3, which equals 5 meters. Point Y is 5 meters deeper than point X.

Step 3 — Calculate the pressure difference. Pressure difference equals 800 times 10 times 5, which equals 40,000 Pa (pascals).

Step 4 — Determine which point has higher pressure. Because pressure increases as you go deeper, point Y — which is deeper — has the higher pressure. The pressure at Y exceeds the pressure at X by 40,000 Pa.

Conceptual check: This result makes sense because a deeper point has more fluid sitting above it, so the weight of that extra fluid column creates the additional pressure.

questions.q_text: The result that pressure increases with depth comes from analyzing a thin horizontal slab of fluid at rest. Which three forces are balanced in that analysis?
options: A. Pressure from below pushing up, pressure from above pushing down, and the weight of the slab pulling down
B. Pressure from below pushing up, pressure from above pushing up, and the weight of the slab pulling down
C. Pressure from the sides pushing inward, atmospheric pressure pushing down, and buoyancy pushing up
D. Viscous drag from below, viscous drag from above, and the weight of the slab

questions.q_text: A diver descends from 5 meters below the surface of a lake to 15 meters below the surface. The water has a density of 1000 kilograms per cubic meter and g is 10 meters per second squared. By how much does the pressure on the diver increase?
Pascal's Law says a pressure change at one point spreads equally throughout a liquid. Which property of the liquid is most essential for this to work?
options: A. The liquid must be very dense
B. The liquid must be incompressible, so distances between points do not change
C. The liquid must be at a high temperature
D. The liquid must be in a very large container

questions.q_text: A sealed container is completely filled with water. You press down on one side and increase the pressure there by 50 pascals. By how much does the pressure change at a point on the opposite side of the container, at the same depth?
options: A. Less than 50 pascals, because some pressure is lost travelling through the liquid
B. Exactly 50 pascals
C. More than 50 pascals, because the liquid amplifies pressure
D. Zero, because pressure changes only act locally

questions.q_text: A hydraulic lift has a narrow piston with an area of 0.01 square metres and a wide piston with an area of 0.5 square metres. A mechanic pushes down on the narrow piston with a force of 200 newtons. What is the force produced on the wide piston, and how does this illustrate Pascal's Law?
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Find the pressure increase created by the mechanic. Pressure equals force divided by area, so the pressure increase is 200 divided by 0.01, which equals 20,000 pascals.

Step 2 — Apply Pascal's Law. This pressure increase of 20,000 pascals is transmitted equally to every point in the liquid, including the surface of the wide piston.

Step 3 — Find the force on the wide piston. Force equals pressure multiplied by area, so the force is 20,000 multiplied by 0.5, which equals 10,000 newtons.

Conclusion — A modest push of 200 newtons on the narrow side produces 10,000 newtons on the wide side — a 50 times multiplication of force. This is Pascal's Law in action: the same pressure increase, acting over a much larger area, produces a proportionally larger force.

questions.q_text: In a hydraulic lift, the wide piston has 20 times the area of the narrow piston. The wide piston therefore produces 20 times the force. If the narrow piston is pushed down by 60 centimetres, how far does the wide piston move upward?
options: A. 1,200 centimetres, because the larger piston moves more
B. 60 centimetres, because both pistons move the same distance
C. 3 centimetres, because the larger piston moves proportionally less
D. 0 centimetres, because the force is used up lifting the load

questions.q_text: Two points in a stationary liquid are separated by a vertical distance. You increase the pressure at the surface of the liquid. What happens to the pressure difference between those two points?
options: A. The pressure difference increases, because the deeper point is pushed down harder
B. The pressure difference decreases, because the added pressure spreads out
C. The pressure difference stays exactly the same, because both points rise by the same amount
D. The pressure difference becomes zero, because Pascal's Law equalises all pressures

questions.q_text: In a Venturi tube, water flows from a wide section into a narrow section. Compared to the wide section, what happens to the water speed and pressure in the narrow section?
options: A. Speed increases and pressure increases
B. Speed decreases and pressure decreases
C. Speed increases and pressure decreases
D. Speed decreases and pressure increases

questions.q_text: Torricelli's theorem says the speed of water leaving a hole at the bottom of a tank equals the square root of 2gh, where h is the height of the water surface above the hole. A student notices this is the same formula as the speed of a ball dropped from height h under gravity. Which statement best explains why these two situations give the same formula?
options: A. It is a coincidence with no physical meaning
B. Both situations involve the same conversion of gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy
C. Water and solid objects always obey the same equations of motion
D. The continuity equation forces the two speeds to be equal

questions.q_text: A large tank has a small hole at its base. The water surface is 5 metres above the hole, and both the surface and the hole are open to the atmosphere. Using Torricelli's theorem, what is the speed of water leaving the hole? Take g as 10 metres per second squared.
options: A. 5 metres per second
B. 10 metres per second
C. 50 metres per second
D. 100 metres per second

questions.q_text: A cricket ball moves through air at 30 metres per second. Due to spin, the air speed on one side of the ball is 36 metres per second and on the other side is 24 metres per second. The density of air is 1.2 kilograms per cubic metre. Using Bernoulli's equation, calculate the pressure difference between the two sides of the ball, and explain which side has higher pressure.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the two sides.
Let Side A be where air moves at 36 m/s (spin adds to airflow) and Side B be where air moves at 24 m/s (spin opposes airflow).

Step 2 — Apply Bernoulli's equation between the two sides at the same height, so the gravity terms cancel.
Pressure on Side B plus one-half times density times speed on Side B squared equals Pressure on Side A plus one-half times density times speed on Side A squared.

Step 3 — Rearrange for the pressure difference.
Pressure on Side B minus Pressure on Side A equals one-half times density times (speed on Side A squared minus speed on Side B squared).

Step 4 — Substitute values.
Speed on Side A squared = 36 times 36 = 1296 metres squared per second squared.
Speed on Side B squared = 24 times 24 = 576 metres squared per second squared.
Difference of squares = 1296 minus 576 = 720 metres squared per second squared.

Pressure difference = one-half times 1.2 times 720 = 0.6 times 720 = 432 Pascals.

Step 5 — Interpret the result.
Side B (slower air, 24 m/s) has the higher pressure, and Side A (faster air, 36 m/s) has the lower pressure. The net pressure difference of 432 Pascals acts from Side B toward Side A, pushing the ball sideways toward the faster-moving air side. This is the aerodynamic force responsible for the ball swinging in the air.

questions.q_text: An aspirator pump forces air through a narrow constriction to suck liquid up from a container below. Which physical principle is directly responsible for the liquid being drawn upward?
options: A. The high pressure created in the narrow section pushes the liquid up
B. The low pressure created in the narrow section allows atmospheric pressure to push the liquid up
C. The continuity equation requires liquid to replace the air that has passed through
D. Gravity pulls the fast-moving air downward, creating a vacuum above the liquid

questions.q_text: When you place your thumb over the end of a garden hose and partially block the opening, the water shoots out much faster. A student claims this happens because placing your thumb increases the water pressure inside the hose, which pushes the water out faster. Is this explanation consistent with the equation of continuity?
options: A. Yes — increased pressure is exactly what the equation of continuity predicts
B. No — the equation of continuity explains the speed increase purely through the reduction in cross-sectional area, not a change in pressure
C. No — the equation of continuity predicts the water should slow down when the area is reduced
D. Yes — the equation of continuity and pressure increase both independently cause the speed to rise

questions.q_text: A river narrows from a wide, slow-moving section into a gorge. Assuming the water is incompressible and the depth stays roughly the same, what do you expect to happen to the river's speed in the gorge?
options: A. The speed decreases because the water has less room
B. The speed increases because the cross-sectional area is smaller
C. The speed stays the same because the same water is flowing
D. The speed increases because pressure drops in the gorge

questions.q_text: Water flows through a pipe that suddenly narrows so that the cross-sectional area is reduced to one quarter of its original value. What happens to the speed of the water in the narrow section?
options: A. The speed stays the same
B. The speed doubles
C. The speed quadruples
D. The speed is reduced to one quarter

questions.q_text: Water enters a pipe at point A where the cross-sectional area is 0.08 square metres, moving at a speed of 3 metres per second. The pipe narrows to a cross-sectional area of 0.02 square metres at point B. Using the equation of continuity, find the speed of the water at point B.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Write the equation of continuity: area at A times speed at A equals area at B times speed at B, or A1 times v1 equals A2 times v2.

Step 2 — Substitute the known values: 0.08 times 3 equals 0.02 times v2.

Step 3 — Calculate the left side: 0.08 times 3 equals 0.24 cubic metres per second.

Step 4 — Solve for v2: v2 equals 0.24 divided by 0.02, which gives v2 equals 12 metres per second.

The water at point B moves at 12 metres per second. Notice that the area decreased by a factor of 4 (from 0.08 to 0.02), so the speed increased by a factor of 4 (from 3 to 12 metres per second), exactly as the equation of continuity predicts.

questions.q_text: The equation of continuity is fundamentally an expression of which physical principle?
options: A. Conservation of energy
B. Conservation of momentum
C. Conservation of mass
D. Newton's second law

questions.q_text: Water flows horizontally through a pipe. At a wide section, the pressure is 200,000 pascals and the water speed is 2 meters per second. At a narrow section, the pressure drops to 180,000 pascals. The density of water is 1000 kilograms per cubic meter. Using the Bernoulli equation, find the speed of the water at the narrow section.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Write the Bernoulli equation for two points on the same horizontal level (so the height terms cancel out):

P1 + one half times rho times v1 squared = P2 + one half times rho times v2 squared

Step 2 — Rearrange to solve for v2 squared:

one half times rho times v2 squared = P1 - P2 + one half times rho times v1 squared

v2 squared = (2 divided by rho) times (P1 - P2) + v1 squared

Step 3 — Substitute the known values:

P1 - P2 = 200,000 - 180,000 = 20,000 pascals
rho = 1000 kg per cubic meter
v1 = 2 m/s

v2 squared = (2 divided by 1000) times 20,000 + (2 squared)
v2 squared = 40 + 4
v2 squared = 44

Step 4 — Take the square root:

v2 = square root of 44 ≈ 6.63 meters per second

The water speed at the narrow section is approximately 6.63 meters per second. Notice that the pressure dropped and the speed increased, exactly as Bernoulli predicts.

questions.q_text: When you run a hot shower, the curtain tends to get pulled inward toward the water stream. Which principle best explains this?
options: A. Hot steam condenses on the curtain and makes it heavier, pulling it down and inward
B. The fast-moving air and water stream inside the shower has lower pressure than the still air outside, so the curtain is pushed inward
C. The water splashing on the curtain exerts a direct force that pushes it inward
D. The curtain is attracted to the warm water by a temperature-driven pressure gradient

questions.q_text: Water flows through a pipe that rises to a higher elevation while keeping the same diameter throughout. Assuming steady, nonviscous flow, what must be true about the pressure at the higher section compared to the lower section?
options: A. The pressure is higher at the top because the water has more potential energy
B. The pressure is the same at both sections because the diameter did not change
C. The pressure is lower at the top because the increase in gravitational potential energy must be compensated by a drop in pressure
D. The pressure is lower at the top only if the fluid speeds up

questions.q_text: A student claims: 'If I make a pipe wider, the fluid slows down, so by Bernoulli's equation the pressure must go up.' A second student says: 'That reasoning only works if the pipe stays at the same height.' Who is correct?
options: A. The first student is fully correct — widening always raises pressure regardless of height
B. The second student is correct — the pressure increase only holds if there is no change in height between the two sections
C. Both students are wrong — widening a pipe has no effect on pressure
D. The first student is correct about the direction of the pressure change, and the second student adds an important condition that must also be satisfied for that conclusion to hold cleanly

questions.q_text: A horizontal pipe narrows from a wide section to a narrow section. The fluid speed increases in the narrow section. What happens to the fluid pressure in the narrow section compared to the wide section?
options: A. The pressure increases because the fluid is squeezed together
B. The pressure decreases because faster flow corresponds to lower pressure
C. The pressure stays the same because the pipe is horizontal
D. The pressure decreases because the fluid density increases

questions.q_text: In steady flow, fluid inside a tube of flow never mixes with fluid in a neighboring tube of flow, even though there is no physical wall between them. What is the reason for this?
options: A. The pressure difference between tubes pushes fluid back if it tries to cross.
B. Fluid in the center of a pipe always moves faster, creating a barrier.
C. Streamlines never cross, so a particle following one streamline can never move onto a streamline belonging to a different tube.
D. Turbulence at the boundary between tubes prevents any mixing.

questions.q_text: In steady flow, a streamline curves gently through a fluid. At a particular point on the streamline, what tells you the exact direction in which a fluid particle is moving at that moment?
options: A. The chord connecting the starting point of the streamline to that point.
B. The tangent to the streamline at that point.
C. The normal (perpendicular) to the streamline at that point.
D. The average direction of the entire streamline from start to finish.

questions.q_text: Why is it impossible for two streamlines to cross each other in steady flow?
options: A. The fluid would speed up too much at the crossing point, causing turbulence.
B. A particle at the crossing point would have two different directions of motion at the same time, which cannot happen.
C. Streamlines only exist in straight pipes, so they never get the chance to cross.
D. The pressure at a crossing point would become zero, which violates physical laws.

questions.q_text: A student says: 'In steady flow, every particle in the fluid moves at the same speed.' Is this correct, and why?
options: A. Yes, because steady flow means the entire fluid moves as one uniform block.
B. No, because in steady flow the velocity at each fixed point stays constant over time, but different points in the fluid can have different velocities.
C. Yes, because streamlines are parallel, so all particles must travel at identical speeds.
D. No, because steady flow actually allows the velocity at a point to change slowly over time.

questions.q_text: Water flows through a narrow pipe at low speed. A tiny dye particle is injected at point P inside the pipe. A second dye particle is injected at the same point P a few seconds later. Describe the paths of the two particles and explain what this tells you about the type of flow. Then explain what would change if the water speed were increased dramatically.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the flow type at low speed. Because the water moves slowly, the flow is steady (streamline) flow. In steady flow, the velocity at any fixed point does not change over time.

Step 2 — Describe the paths of the two dye particles. The first particle injected at P follows a specific path — its line of flow — through the pipe. Because the flow is steady, the velocity at P is the same when the second particle arrives there. The second particle therefore follows exactly the same path as the first, arriving at every downstream point with the same speed and direction. Both particles trace identical paths.

Step 3 — Connect to streamlines. Since every particle through P follows the same path, that path is a well-defined streamline. The tangent to the streamline at any point gives the direction of motion of all particles passing through that point.

Step 4 — What changes at very high speed. If the water speed is increased dramatically, the flow becomes turbulent. Now the velocity at point P changes from moment to moment — in both magnitude and direction. The first dye particle might curve to the left; the second, arriving at P a moment later, might shoot upward or spiral unpredictably. The two paths are no longer identical, and there are no longer well-defined streamlines. The orderly, predictable structure of steady flow breaks down entirely.

questions.q_text: The main reason physicists combine all three assumptions — incompressible, nonviscous, and irrotational — when studying fluid flow is that together they do which of the following?
options: A. Make the fluid behave exactly like a solid, which is easier to model
B. Eliminate the need to track individual fluid particles entirely
C. Simplify the governing equations to a point where they become mathematically solvable
D. Guarantee that the fluid moves in straight lines only

questions.q_text: A student says that assuming a fluid is nonviscous means we are ignoring which physical effect?
options: A. The compressibility of the fluid under pressure
B. The internal friction between layers of the fluid
C. The spinning motion of fluid particles
D. The variation in fluid density from place to place

questions.q_text: You observe water being stirred in a circular pattern, creating a small whirlpool in the center. Which of the three key assumptions described in this topic does this situation violate?
options: A. Incompressibility
B. Nonviscous flow
C. Irrotational flow
D. Constant pressure

questions.q_text: Which of the following scenarios is the incompressibility assumption LEAST likely to be valid?
options: A. Water flowing through a garden hose
B. Oil moving slowly through a pipe
C. Air being compressed rapidly inside a bicycle pump
D. A river flowing over a shallow bed

questions.q_text: A fluid flows steadily through a pipe. Measurements show that the density of the fluid is the same at every point along the pipe and does not change over time. A dye injected into the fluid shows that small fluid elements translate and deform as they move, but do not spin about their own centers. The fluid is also known to have negligible internal friction. For each of the three assumptions discussed in this topic — incompressible, nonviscous, and irrotational — state whether it applies to this fluid and explain your reasoning using the observations given.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Incompressible: The problem states that the density is the same at every point and does not change over time. This is exactly the definition of an incompressible fluid. So yes, the incompressibility assumption applies.

Step 2 — Nonviscous: The problem tells us the fluid has negligible internal friction. Viscosity is internal friction between fluid layers, so negligible internal friction means we can treat the fluid as nonviscous. This assumption applies.

Step 3 — Irrotational: The dye observation shows that fluid elements translate (move from place to place) and deform (change shape), but do not spin about their own centers. Irrotational flow means fluid particles have no net rotational or spinning motion. Since the dye confirms there is no spinning of individual fluid elements, the irrotational assumption applies.

Conclusion: All three assumptions — incompressible, nonviscous, and irrotational — are satisfied by this fluid based on the given observations. This means the simplified equations of irrotational flow can be applied to analyze this situation.

questions.q_text: You pour water into a spherical bowl and it takes the bowl's shape, but the amount of water you poured in does not change. Which of the following best explains this behavior in terms of intermolecular forces?
options: A. Water has strong intermolecular forces that resist any change in shape but weak forces that allow volume to change freely.
B. Water has weak intermolecular forces that allow shape to change easily, but those same forces are strong enough to resist significant changes in volume.
C. Water has no intermolecular forces, so both its shape and volume adjust to match the container.
D. Water has the same intermolecular force strength as a solid, which is why its volume stays fixed.

questions.q_text: In our idealized nonviscous liquid model, two neighboring layers of liquid slide past each other. What does the nonviscous assumption tell us about the force between these layers?
options: A. There is no force at all between the two layers.
B. The force acts along the surface between the layers, causing friction.
C. The force acts perpendicular to the surface between the layers, with no friction along it.
D. The force acts at 45 degrees to the surface, splitting equally between friction and pressure.

questions.q_text: When we say a liquid is incompressible in our model, what exactly are we assuming stays constant?
options: A. The pressure throughout the liquid
B. The temperature of the liquid
C. The density of the liquid
D. The speed at which the liquid flows

questions.q_text: A student has two sealed syringes — one filled with water and one filled with air. She pushes the plunger of each with the same force. Explain, using the concept of intermolecular forces and the properties of fluids, why the air syringe compresses noticeably while the water syringe barely compresses at all. Then state which of our two simplifying assumptions for liquids this observation supports.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Intermolecular forces in each fluid: In air (a gas), the intermolecular forces between molecules are very small. The molecules are already far apart and not strongly attracted to each other. In water (a liquid), the intermolecular forces are significantly stronger, holding molecules much closer together. Step 2 — Response to applied pressure: When the student pushes the plunger on the air syringe, the applied force easily overcomes the weak intermolecular forces, allowing the gas molecules to be pushed closer together. The volume decreases noticeably and the density of the air increases — the gas is compressible. When she pushes the plunger on the water syringe, the stronger intermolecular forces resist the molecules being pushed closer together. The volume barely changes, meaning the density of the water stays nearly constant — the liquid resists compression strongly. Step 3 — Connecting to our simplifying assumption: This observation directly supports the incompressibility assumption. In our model of liquids, we assume the density remains constant regardless of changes in pressure. The water syringe experiment shows this is a very good approximation for real liquids like water, because even a large applied force produces almost no change in volume or density.

questions.q_text: A student says that only liquids count as fluids because gases don't flow in a controlled way. Is the student correct, and why?
options: A. Yes, because fluids are defined by having a fixed volume, which only liquids have.
B. No, because any substance that can flow is a fluid, so both liquids and gases are fluids.
C. Yes, because gases change density too easily to be considered true fluids.
D. No, because fluids are defined by having very strong intermolecular forces, which gases lack.

questions.q_text: A beaker of water is pushed horizontally with a constant acceleration of 5 meters per second squared. Taking g as 10 meters per second squared, find the angle that the free surface of the water makes with the horizontal.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall the result for horizontal acceleration. The tangent of the tilt angle equals the horizontal acceleration divided by g. So: tangent of angle = a divided by g = 5 divided by 10 = 0.5. Step 2: Find the angle. The angle equals the inverse tangent of 0.5, which is approximately 26.6 degrees. So the free surface tilts at about 26.6 degrees from the horizontal, with the back of the beaker sitting higher than the front.

questions.q_text: A beaker of water accelerates horizontally on a frictionless surface. Which of the following correctly describes what happens to the free surface of the water?
options: A. The surface remains flat and horizontal because gravity still acts straight down
B. The surface tilts so that the front of the beaker has a higher water level than the back
C. The surface tilts so that the back of the beaker has a higher water level than the front
D. The surface becomes curved, rising at both edges and dipping in the middle

questions.q_text: Suppose a sealed container of liquid is in free fall — accelerating downward at exactly g. A student claims the pressure difference between any two points inside the liquid becomes zero. Is the student correct, and why?
options: A. No, because gravity still acts on the liquid regardless of the container's motion
B. Yes, because the effective gravity is g minus g, which equals zero, so there is no pressure variation with depth
C. No, because pressure difference depends on horizontal separation, not vertical
D. Yes, but only if the two points are at the same horizontal level

questions.q_text: A container of liquid is inside an elevator accelerating upward at acceleration a. Compared to when the elevator is stationary, how does the pressure difference between a point near the bottom and a point near the top of the liquid change?
options: A. It decreases, because the upward acceleration partially cancels gravity
B. It stays the same, because pressure depends only on depth and density
C. It increases, because the effective gravity becomes g plus a
D. It becomes zero, because the liquid is in free motion

questions.q_text: An object is fully submerged in a liquid inside a container that is accelerating upward with acceleration a. How does the buoyant force on the object compare to when the container is stationary?
options: A. It is smaller, because the object's weight effectively increases
B. It is the same, because buoyancy depends only on the volume of displaced fluid
C. It is larger, because the effective gravity acting on the displaced fluid is g plus a
D. It is zero, because the upward acceleration cancels the effect of gravity

questions.q_text: A student says: 'Fluid mechanics must use completely different laws of physics from the ones we learned for solid objects.' What is the most accurate response to this claim?
options: A. The student is correct — fluids obey special fluid laws, not Newton's laws
B. The student is wrong — every tiny particle of fluid obeys Newton's laws, but tracking all those particles simultaneously makes the mathematics enormously complex
C. The student is partially right — Newton's laws apply only when the fluid flows smoothly without turbulence
D. The student is wrong — fluids are so complex that no known laws of physics apply to them reliably

questions.q_text: Why is it so difficult to predict the exact path of a single water droplet in a waterfall, even though we know the laws governing its motion?
options: A. Because water droplets are too small for Newton's laws to apply to them
B. Because gravity does not act consistently on moving water
C. Because each droplet is constantly being pushed and pulled by forces from surrounding water, rocks, and air, making the combined calculation enormously complicated
D. Because the droplet moves too fast for any equations to keep up with it

questions.q_text: A student watches smoke rising from a candle and says: 'I know Newton's second law — force equals mass times acceleration. So if I know the mass of one smoke particle and all the forces on it right now, I can easily calculate exactly where it will be in ten seconds.' Carefully explain whether the student is right or wrong, and why.
questions.answer: The student is partially right but mostly wrong in their conclusion. They are correct that Newton's second law applies to every smoke particle — force equals mass times acceleration holds for each tiny particle at every moment. However, the student is wrong to say this makes the calculation easy. Here is why: each smoke particle is being pushed by forces from air currents around it, gravity pulling it down, heat rising from the flame below, and the movements of all the neighboring particles surrounding it. Each of those neighboring particles is itself being pushed by its own set of neighbors, and so on. To truly predict where one particle ends up, you would need to simultaneously track the forces on every particle in the system, because they all influence each other. The number of particles in even a small puff of smoke is astronomically large. So while the law itself is simple and familiar, applying it to every interacting particle at every moment in time makes the actual calculation enormously and practically impossibly complex. This is the central challenge of fluid mechanics: the governing law is simple, but the prediction of real motion is extremely hard.

questions.q_text: When physicists assume that a fluid flows smoothly without turbulence in order to solve a problem, what kind of scientific thinking does this represent?
options: A. Sloppy thinking, because ignoring turbulence means the answer will always be wrong
B. A deliberate simplification that makes the problem manageable, while accepting that real fluids can be more complex
C. A proven fact, because all real fluids always flow smoothly under normal conditions
D. An admission that Newton's laws do not work for fluids

questions.q_text: The explanation says that keeping in mind the limitations of simplified fluid models is 'a sign of good scientific thinking.' Which of the following best explains why this humility is valuable in science?
options: A. Because it means scientists never have to commit to any answer
B. Because it reminds scientists that their models are useful approximations, and that real phenomena may be richer and more complex than the model captures
C. Because complicated problems should always be avoided in favour of simpler ones
D. Because admitting difficulty means you do not have to solve the problem at all

questions.q_text: A steel ship floats even though solid steel is much denser than water. Which statement best explains why?
options: A. The ship moves fast enough that water pressure holds it up
B. Steel becomes less dense when shaped into thin sheets
C. The ship's overall density — including all the hollow air-filled space inside — is less than the density of water
D. The buoyant force depends on the weight of the ship, not the weight of displaced water

questions.q_text: A rectangular block of wood has a density of 600 kilograms per cubic metre. It is placed in fresh water, which has a density of 1000 kilograms per cubic metre. What fraction of the block's volume is submerged when it floats in equilibrium?
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Set up the equilibrium condition. When the block floats, the buoyant force equals the block's weight. So: weight of displaced water = weight of block.

Step 2 — Express both sides in terms of volume. Let V be the total volume of the block, and let V_sub be the submerged volume. The weight of the block is: density of wood times V times g = 600 times V times g. The weight of displaced water is: density of water times V_sub times g = 1000 times V_sub times g.

Step 3 — Set them equal and solve. 1000 times V_sub times g = 600 times V times g. Dividing both sides by g and by 1000: V_sub = (600 divided by 1000) times V = 0.6 times V.

Step 4 — State the answer. The fraction of the block that is submerged is 0.6, or 60 percent. This makes intuitive sense: because the wood is 60 percent as dense as water, it needs to displace a volume of water equal to 60 percent of its own volume to balance its weight.

questions.q_text: An object is submerged in a liquid and the buoyant force acting on it is 12 newtons. What can you conclude about the weight of the fluid displaced by the object?
options: A. It is less than 12 newtons, because the object is denser than the fluid
B. It equals 12 newtons, by Archimedes' principle
C. It is greater than 12 newtons, because some force is lost to friction
D. It cannot be determined without knowing the object's density

questions.q_text: A solid metal cube is fully submerged in water. You then push it deeper so it is twice as far below the surface. How does the buoyant force change?
options: A. It doubles, because the pressure at greater depth is higher
B. It stays the same, because the volume of displaced water has not changed
C. It decreases, because the water above pushes down harder
D. It increases slightly, because water density increases with depth

questions.q_text: Archimedes' principle is derived by imagining a blob of fluid replaced by a solid object and using the fact that the blob was in equilibrium. Which condition is essential for this derivation to hold?
